Will Taiwan vote to revive nuclear power – and why does that matter for AI? | Nuclear Energy News | Al Jazeera
Share Will Taiwan vote to revive nuclear power – and why does that matter for AI? on social media
Taiwanese protesters mimic escaping from a nuclear explosion, December 4, 2021 [Lam Yik Fei/Getty Images]
Voters in Taiwan are set to decide whether to bring back nuclear power – 18 months after its last operational reactor was shut down.
A referendum on the issue is being held alongside local elections on Saturday. It is the island’s fourth vote on nuclear power in just eight years.
list 1 of 3Xi Jinping says Taiwan’s ‘complete reunification’ with China will happen
list 2 of 3Asian stock markets tumble as AI bubble fears mount
list 3 of 3Asia’s markets dive as return of Nvidia’s Huang fails to quell AI doubts
It comes as demand for electricity to fuel the country’s burgeoning computer chip industry soars and concern grows about how Taiwan would keep its lights on if China, which claims the island as its own territory, cut it off amid escalating tensions.
Voters are being asked whether the government should return to using nuclear power to boost the economy. That would mean abolishing the country’s longstanding “nuclear-free homeland” policy.
The opposition Kuomintang (KMT) proposed the referendum and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) is also backing it. The legislature approved the referendum in August and the Central Election Commission signed it off on August 28.
To pass, ‘yes’ votes must outnumber ‘no’ votes and exceed a quarter of all eligible voters.
The ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), which has long had a policy of no nuclear power in its mandate, is urging ‘no’. DPP legislator Chen Pei-yu called the referendum unnecessary, saying lawmakers could change the policy by amending existing laws instead.
Taiwan once relied heavily on nuclear power. In 1985, its three plants produced 52 percent of the nation’s electricity.
Nuclear power then became one of the most partisan issues in Taiwanese politics. Lev Nachman, an assistant professor at the Graduate Institute of National Development at National Taiwan University, said the divide goes back to the DPP’s founding.
“There was a major group of environmentalists that were part of the party that were very anti-nuclear,” Nachman told Al Jazeera. The nuclear industry, by contrast, was built and run under the KMT.
Polarisation turned that into “a very green-versus-blue issue”, Nachman said, referring to the colours of the DPP and the KMT.
Safety fears run deep. Nachman said Taiwan watched the 2011 Fukushima nuclear plant meltdown in neighbouring Japan very closely.
“There is this sort of fear of any sort of nuclear reaction that would ever happen in Taiwan would just devastate the entire island,” he said. Active geological fault lines run across Taiwan and the question of how to dispose of nuclear waste remains unresolved.
The DPP has governed since 2016, partly on a pledge to phase out nuclear power. In May last year, Taiwan shut down its last reactor at Maanshan in Pingtung County.
Why is nuclear power back on the agenda?
Public opinion has been mixed in three previous referendums. In 2018, voters opted to scrap a legal deadline for phasing out nuclear power. But in 2021, they rejected restarting construction on an unfinished fourth nuclear plant. In August last year, a majority vote to restart the Maanshan plant was voided due to low turnout.
Now, nuclear power is back on the agenda because surging electricity demand from Taiwan’s semiconductor and AI industries, along with growing fears about energy security and over-reliance on imported fuel, have renewed the debate over how the island keeps the lights on in an emergency.
According to the Ministry of Economic Affairs, Taiwan imports more than 97 percent of its energy. Natural gas generates about 43 percent of its electricity and coal about 35 percent. Both arrive by ship.
Taiwan only has about 11 days of liquefied natural gas (LNG) in reserve. Japan and South Korea hold between 14 and 20 days.
“There’s two sides to it,” Nachman said. The first is energy security: “If China actually blockades Taiwan and cuts off access to the outside world, then Taiwan only has so much energy it can rely on.”
The second is the chip industry, which requires huge amounts of power and “that’s only going to increase over time”, he said.
The war with Iran this year has added to the pressure by disrupting LNG shipments from the Middle East.
Will the ruling party change its stance?
The DPP has already started to shift. In March, President William Lai Ching-te said the government would begin the process of restarting the Maanshan and Kuosheng plants. He cited AI-driven demand and conflicts abroad causing disruption to energy supplies.
On September 24, the Nuclear Safety Commission approved state-owned Taipower’s restart plan for Maanshan. Further safety assessments are still needed before it can operate again.
Nachman said Lai has tried to push his party to rethink its “very dogmatic anti-nuclear stance”. The question is whether DPP voters have come around.
Nuclear power is not Taiwan’s first choice for filling the gap, however. “Investment in LNG – that’s still Taiwan’s kind of number one goal,” Nachman said.
How important is Taiwan’s microchip industry?
Taiwan is the most important link in the global AI supply chain.
It makes more than 90 percent of the world’s most advanced semiconductors, nearly all of them at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). TSMC has more than 60 percent of the global contract chipmaking market.
Its customers include Nvidia – the world’s most valuable semiconductor company – AMD and Apple. TSMC makes Nvidia’s Blackwell and Rubin AI processors, and Taiwanese firms such as Foxconn and Quanta build most of the world’s AI servers.
That uses huge amounts of electricity and water. In September, Taiwan’s semiconductor industry used more than 4.5 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity for the first time. That was up 11.55 percent from a year earlier, driven by AI demand.
S&P Global estimated that TSMC alone used about 8 percent of Taiwan’s electricity in 2023. That share could rise to almost 24 percent by 2030, it added.
Nachman cautioned against seeing the referendum only through the demand for microchips and semiconductors. “In today’s media, Taiwan has become a single issue, just about semiconductors,” he said. “For a lot of people in Taiwan, the semiconductors aren’t even the priority. It really is the security side.”
Will China object to Taiwan having nuclear power?
Probably not. Beijing does not appear to have commented on the referendum itself.
“The nuclear issue is a completely separate issue from anything related to China,” Nachman said. “It’s much more a matter of domestic politics.”
China has, however, used Taiwan’s energy weakness in its messaging. In March, Chen Binhua, a spokesman for China’s Taiwan Affairs Office, said closer integration with China could help solve Taiwan’s energy problems. He pointed to the island’s reliance on oil and gas from the Middle East.
Taipei rejects unification with Beijing. Analysts writing in The Diplomat called the offer an exercise in optics.
However, it remains a top priority for China. During a speech in Beijing on November 12, President Xi Jinping once again stated that Taiwan and China must be reunified.
The referendum is about civilian power reactors, not weapons. Asked whether Taiwan might seek a nuclear weapon, Nachman said: “No, of course not. This is just about nuclear power.”
Taiwan did secretly pursue nuclear weapons in the 1970s and 1980s. The programme was shut down in 1988 under US pressure, after a senior nuclear scientist, Chang Hsien-yi, defected to the United States.
Since then, Taiwan’s leaders have consistently stated that they will not seek nuclear weapons. Its nuclear facilities are inspected under an arrangement between Taiwan, the US and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).
The bigger worry is a blockade by China if it seeks to press reunification in the future. Nachman said large military drills and naval patrols China has held around Taiwan since US House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit in 2022 have all rehearsed one.
Will the referendum pass and what happens next?
Nachman said he is sceptical. “We keep doing it over and over again and it still doesn’t usually pass,” he said. “So my expectations are actually fairly low.”
The outcome will depend on DPP supporters. “It’s really more a matter of whether or not green voters have come around to it,” Nachman said.
If the referendum does pass, he said Lai and the DPP “would probably be largely okay with it”.
The restart process is already under way either way. Supporters say reactors could be running again within 18 months to three years. Opponents say a restart could take five to 10 years and cost several hundred billion New Taiwan dollars.
Results are expected on Saturday night.

**NEWS** | Nov. 25, 2026

# Tentara Nasional Indonesia Angkatan Laut, U.S. Navy commence CARAT Indonesia 2026

By Lt. Camillia Nguyen, Commander, Destroyer Squadron 7 Public Affairs

 SURABAYA, Indonesia–
Maritime defense forces from U.S. 7th Fleet and Tentara Nasional Indonesia Angkatan Laut (TNI-AL) convened in Surabaya, Nov. 25, to commence Cooperation Afloat Readiness and Training (CARAT) Indonesia.

The 32nd iteration of CARAT Indonesia launched with an opening ceremony, building upon previous maritime exercises and operations between the U.S. and Indonesia. CARAT is a maritime exercise designed to promote regional security cooperation, maintain and strengthen maritime partnerships, and enhance interoperability among participating forces.

“CARAT represents a commitment shared by the United States and Indonesia to promote maritime security and readiness across the Indo-Pacific,” said Chris Green, U.S. Consul General in Surabaya. “After more than 30 years, CARAT continues to enhance our ability to work side-by-side across a wide range of naval competencies.”

Avenger-class mine countermeasures ship USS Warrior (MCM 10) from Commander, Task Force (CTF) 77 arrived in Indonesia, Nov. 25, to kick off preliminary events. The sea-phase of the exercise will also feature a P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol and reconnaissance aircraft from CTF-72, as well as three TNI-AL Sigma-class corvettes, Fani-class mine countermeasures vessels KRI Pulau Fani (MCMV 731) and KRI Pulau Fanildo (MCMV 732), two Airbus AS656 Panther helicopters, and one TNI-AL CN 235 aircraft from TNI-AL. The sea-phase of this iteration will feature anti-submarine warfare drills, mine countermeasures best practices, and surface action group coordination to exercise command and control across units.

Additional personnel and staff supporting CARAT Indonesia 2026 include Commander, Destroyer Squadron (DESRON) 7, the U.S. 7th Fleet Band, and subject matter experts from CTF-73, CTF-75, and Naval Information Warfare Center Pacific. Subject matter expert exchange (SMEE) topics will include aviation, cyber, salvage diving, explosive ordnance disposal, and **U.S.–TNI-AL** combined musical performances. The SMEEs, held ashore in Surabaya, will facilitate information-sharing and promote interoperability at sea through building people-to-people relationships.

“We are grateful to our Indonesian partners for their warm welcome and hospitality in Surabaya,” said U.S. Navy Capt. Alfonza White, chief of staff, CTF-76, and head of delegation. “CARAT strengthens our coordination, builds mutual trust, and helps us preserve a free and open Indo-Pacific.”

CARAT is a long-standing exercise series designed to enhance U.S. and partner forces abilities to operate together in response to shared maritime challenges in the region.

As the U.S. Navy’s forward-deployed DESRON in Southeast Asia, DESRON-7 serves as the primary tactical and operational commander of assigned ships in the Southeast Asia area of operations.

U.S. 7th Fleet, the Navy’s largest forward-deployed numbered fleet, routinely interacts and operates with allies and partners in preserving a free and open Indo-Pacific.

summary: 中国在亚洲能源安全计划中明显缺席 - 大西洋理事会中国 东亚 能源与环境 地缘政治与能源安全 2026 年 11 月 25 日 • 东部时间上午 10:04 中国在亚洲能源安全计划中明显缺席 霍尔木兹海峡冲击发生九个月后，能源安全已被列入上周日本-东盟和亚太经合组织 (APEC) 峰会的议程。五年来的第二次价格冲击迫使亚洲政策制定者重新考虑能源安全规划和机构，但中国并没有带头，尽管它在地区能源领域发挥着重要作用。
content:
大西洋理事会：亚洲能源安全计划中明显缺席中国
中国东亚 能源与环境 地缘政治与能源安全
2026 年 11 月 25 日 • 上午 10:04（美国东部时间）
中国在亚洲能源安全计划中明显缺席
霍尔木兹海峡地震发生九个月后，能源安全问题被提上上周日本-东盟和亚太经济合作组织 (APEC) 峰会的议程。五年来的第二次价格冲击迫使亚洲政策制定者重新考虑能源安全规划和机构，但中国并没有带头，尽管它在地区能源安全中发挥着重要作用。
中国的优先事项是国内而非地区
作为世界上最大的石油进口国，中国与经历霍尔木兹海峡供应中断的邻国依赖进口的国家有很多共同点。然而，关于新的合作能源安全规划机制和机构的新兴区域政策讨论基本上没有提及这一点。
在过去的八个月里，中国一直专注于国内能源优先事项，其行为有时会损害其他亚洲进口商。美国和以色列袭击伊朗仅一周后，中国就禁止了几乎所有石油产品的出口许可证。中国在随后几个月放松了这些限制，但在柴油和其他燃料库存大幅下降后，十月份北京再次限制产品出口。
中国只是东亚第三大石油产品出口国（仅次于韩国和新加坡），但其出口配额的意外变化改变了市场平衡。例如，2025 年，中国供应了澳大利亚近三分之一的航空燃油进口，因此 3 月份的航空燃油禁令让澳大利亚航空公司纷纷寻找替代品。
更广泛地说，中国缺乏透明度给邻国带来了挑战。其2025年至2026年3月的库存增加支撑了全球石油需求，而炼油厂开工率下降、国内燃料价格上限和出口限制等综合因素导致2月至6月原油进口出现前所未有的下降。分析师指出，中国在石油市场的定价能力源于其原油购买的时间和数量。然而，虽然国内考虑推动了这些决定，但它们往往让中国的邻国围绕其行动进行规划。尽管宣布建立东盟-中国能源合作伙伴关系，但其邻国有理由对中国的承诺持谨慎态度。
在经历了能源危机最初几个月的急剧下降之后，亚洲石油进口已经反弹。但这次中断影响了所有依赖中东石油和天然气的进口商。日本通常 90% 以上的原油从中东进口，因此被迫从美国或拉丁美洲寻找替代品（9 月份，美国原油占日本进口量的 27%，高于去年的 3%）。通常从中东进口大部分液化石油气的印度已转向美国供应。其他亚洲进口商一直在努力获取石化原料。
进口商正在重新评估他们的供应商关系。正如国际能源署 (IEA) 执行董事法提赫·比罗尔 (Fatih Birol) 在 2026 年 4 月大西洋理事会活动中所说，进口商现在有三个重要目标：“能源来源多元化。能源结构多元化。贸易路线多元化。”对于长期依赖石油的亚洲进口商来说，这是一项艰巨的任务。

China’s conspicuous absence in Asian energy security plans - Atlantic Council
China East Asia Energy & Environment Geopolitics & Energy Security
November 25, 2026 • 10:04am ET
China’s conspicuous absence in Asian energy security plans
Nine months into the Strait of Hormuz shock, energy security was on the agenda at last week’s Japan-ASEAN and Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summits. The second price shock in five years has forced Asian policymakers to rethink energy security planning and institutions—but China is not leading the charge despite its significant role in regional energy security.
China’s priorities are domestic, not regional
As the world’s largest oil importer, China has much in common with neighboring import-dependent countries weathering the Strait of Hormuz supply disruption. Yet it is largely absent from emerging regional policy discussions over new cooperative energy security planning mechanisms and institutions.
Over the past eight months, China has focused on domestic energy priorities—and its actions have sometimes harmed other Asian importers. Only a week after the US and Israeli attack on Iran, China banned export licenses for nearly all petroleum products. China relaxed those restrictions in subsequent months, but in October—after a significant decline in stocks of diesel and other fuels—Beijing again restricted product exports.
China is only the third largest petroleum product exporter in East Asia (after South Korea and Singapore), but unexpected changes to its export quotas alter market balances. For example, China supplied nearly one-third of Australia’s jet fuel imports in 2025, so its March jet fuel ban left Australian airlines scrambling for alternatives.
More broadly, China’s lack of transparency creates challenges for its neighbors. Its 2025-March 2026 inventory builds supported global oil demand, while a combination of lower refinery runs, caps on domestic fuel prices, and export restrictions contributed to an unprecedented decline in crude imports between February and June. Analysts note that China’s pricing power in oil markets stems from the timing and volume of its crude purchases. But while domestic considerations drive these decisions, they often leave China’s neighbors to plan around its actions. Despite the announcement of an ASEAN-China Energy Cooperation Partnership, its neighbors have reason to be cautious about China’s commitment.
After steep declines in the early months of the energy shock, Asian oil imports have rebounded. But the disruption has affected all importers that depend on Middle Eastern oil and gas. Japan typically imports more than 90 percent of its crude oil from the Middle East, so it has been forced to find alternatives from the United States or Latin America (in September, US crude oil accounted for 27 percent of Japan’s imports, up from 3 percent the previous year). India, which normally imports most of its liquefied petroleum gas from the Middle East, has turned to the United States for supply. Other Asian importers have struggled to secure petrochemicals feedstocks.
Importers are re-evaluating their supplier relationships. As International Energy Agency (IEA) Executive Director Fatih Birol stated at an April 2026 Atlantic Council event, importers now have three important objectives: “Diversify from whom you get your energy. Diversify your energy mix. And diversify your trade routes.” This is a difficult task for Asian importers with longstanding dependence on the Middle East, especially those with refineries configured to process crude oil grades from the Gulf and Iraq.
Addressing energy security threats with new institutions
Governments in the region see two major threats to their energy security. First, the shale revolution and the decline in US oil imports have given Washington freer rein to act in ways that can raise their energy costs and jeopardize supplies. And second, that global energy security institutions are no longer fit for purpose, since they were created amid the 1970s oil shocks—when Asia made up a much smaller share of the global economy and global oil and gas consumption.
Energy leaders see a need for new Asian energy security architecture, as governments seek to diversify supplies, build inventories, and explore joint purchasing and sharing mechanisms. Japan aims to lead this effort and has proposed several new programs to bolster energy security.
In Manila last week, leaders from Japan and Southeast Asia updated plans for the Tokyo-led Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC) initiative and the related Partnership on Wide Energy and Resource Resilience Asia (POWERR Asia) framework. The AZEC action plan emphasizes cooperation on emissions reductions, carbon removal, and decarbonization of the transportation sector. Takaichi also proposed a new Asian oil security task force and referred to it as “an Asian version of the International Energy Agency.”
In April, Japan committed up to 1.5 trillion yen ($9.4 billion) under POWERR Asia to support regional procurement of new hydrocarbon supplies, infrastructure to bolster fuel storage and supply chain resilience in Asia, and diversification of energy sources. State institutions including the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC) and Japan Bank for International Cooperation are expected to support these plans that aim to broadly support Asian energy security. In several bills expected to be approved by Japan’s Diet in December, Takaichi’s government tasks JOGMEC with investing in alternative supply infrastructure including bypass pipelines and storage facilities.
At the Japan-ASEAN summit in Manila, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also proposed a new “POWERR Gulf” initiative to enhance cooperation between oil exporters in the Gulf and Asian importers. Inventories will likely be a key focus. Japan in particular is already building on existing joint stockpiling with Gulf national oil companies Saudi Aramco, Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, and Kuwait Petroleum Corporation. On November 20, Saudi Arabia and Japan announced an expanded joint oil stockpiling program. Japan intends to buy 8 million barrels of Saudi crude oil to replenish its stockpiles, and will lend Saudi Arabia new crude oil storage capacity of 16 million barrels, in addition to Aramco’s current 8.2 million barrels of capacity. Under Japan’s current joint oil stockpiling program, Gulf national oil companies lease storage capacity and use it for commercial operations in normal times, but Japanese companies have preferential rights to this crude oil in times of emergency. If the broader region embraces POWERR Gulf, the Gulf-Japan arrangement could become a template for other nations.
Asia will need more than one energy blueprint
The effectiveness of these new energy security initiatives remains to be seen. Japan and other countries in the region will remain highly dependent on the Middle East for crude oil and petroleum products. Energy resource endowments and energy systems also vary greatly across ASEAN countries, so their vulnerabilities and planning principles may differ from one country to the next.
Governments also face a strategic choice. After the second oil and gas price shock in five years, some policymakers in Southeast Asia and South Asia may lean toward more drastic changes in energy policy to emphasize resilience and use of domestic energy resources. Governments in these regions may well decide to direct scarce resources toward expanding electrification, renewable energy generation, battery storage, and grid resilience rather than new fossil fuel infrastructure.
It is notable that Japan is playing such a prominent role in region-wide energy security initiatives. This is unsurprising, since import-dependent Japan excels in long-term energy security planning and policy, including through its Strategic Energy Plans. Some officials and analysts in the broader region, however, worry that the proposed frameworks are too focused on fossil fuels, arguing that new investment should focus on electrification and renewable energy.
Opportunities for energy security leadership
As Asian governments devise new plans and institutions to bolster energy security and resilience, China is both absent and inescapable. China is the world’s largest oil importer, holds the world’s largest oil stockpiles, and is a key customer for nearly all the Gulf countries. More than any other importer, its actions will affect prices and energy security for its neighbors.
Beyond the oil and gas sector, China’s “electrostate” model and its many innovations in electrification, electric vehicle manufacturing, battery technology, and clean energy deployment will be important for Asian countries seeking to cut import dependence and build energy resilience. Yet it is not playing an especially active role in emerging multilateral discussions about how to bolster energy security in Asia. China’s lack of transparency and focus on domestic issues leaves a policy and planning gap that Japan is well positioned to fill.

罗兴亚种族灭绝裁决面临地缘政治考验 - 大西洋理事会
2017 年 8 月 31 日，在孟加拉国特克纳夫，罗兴亚难民在非法越境后被孟加拉国边防卫队扣留，试图躲避暴雨。（路透社/Mohammad Ponir Hossain/档案照片）
康涅狄格州中城——11 月 19 日，国际法院 (ICJ) 裁定缅甸应对罗辛亚社区的种族灭绝负责。这是国际法院首次判定一个国家对种族灭绝负有责任。同日，美国总统特朗普、中国国家主席习近平和俄罗斯总统普京在深圳会晤后发表声明，警告国际刑事法院滥用管辖权。该声明提到了国际刑事法院和“其他类似机构”，其措辞足够广泛，涵盖了联合国主要司法机构国际法院。第二天，缅甸总统发言人在一份声明中提到了三位领导人在国际法庭上的立场，认为国际法院的裁决“不公平”。这表明缅甸执行该判决中规定的措施，特别是对罗兴亚人获得公民身份的保护，可能取决于大国利益所影响的谈判。
这一判决的公民概念表明了真正的利害关系。国际法院承认，剥夺罗兴亚人公民身份是歧视框架的一部分，这与其种族灭绝意图的调查结果有关。尽管如此，它认为给予每个罗辛亚人充分和平等的公民身份“超出了防止另一场种族灭绝的适当保障的范围”。然而，国际法院确实下令采取赔偿措施，包括“确保保护罗兴亚人免受歧视和迫害”。判决书在两处指出，这项措施包括“在获得公民身份方面”和“在获得公民身份方面和在迁徙自由方面保护免受歧视”。
由于法院没有下令缅甸授予罗兴亚人公民身份，罗兴亚人是否真正获得公民身份将取决于在缅甸拥有利益的政府已经参与的政治谈判。从华盛顿对稀土的兴趣到北京的皎漂港口和新德里的加拉丹运输走廊，世界各国政府在就进入其领土和资源问题与缅甸政府进行谈判时，都面临着一个关键选择。他们可以将罗兴亚公民身份纳入政治安排，也可以接受罗兴亚人的持续排斥，以追求自己的战略利益。外部势力应该利用包括贸易在内的影响力，使裁决的实施以及早该实现的公民身份和安全返回之路成为他们支持的任何解决方案的一部分。
国际法院于 2026 年 11 月 19 日在荷兰海牙就指控缅甸对罗兴亚穆斯林少数民族进行种族灭绝的案件作出判决。（路透社/Piroschka van de Wouw）
如果外部势力支持一项让罗兴亚人成为无国籍人的解决方案，那么将他们赶出缅甸的条件将继续存在，而另一次外逃将变得更有可能。法官莱昂纳多·内梅尔·卡尔代拉·布兰特和专案法官纳维·皮莱在联合声明中指出，缅甸确保平等获得公民身份的义务应解读为：

The Rohingya genocide ruling faces a geopolitical test - Atlantic Council
Rohingya refugees try to take shelter from torrential rain as they are held by the Border Guard Bangladesh after illegally crossing the border, in Teknaf, Bangladesh, on August 31, 2017. (REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain/File Photo)
MIDDLETOWN, Connecticut—On November 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya community. It is the first time that the ICJ has held a state responsible for committing genocide. On the same day, US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a declaration after their meeting in Shenzhen that warned against jurisdictional abuse by the International Criminal Court (ICC). The declaration named the ICC and “other similar bodies,” language broad enough to cover the ICJ, the UN’s principal judicial organ. The following day, the spokesperson of the Myanmar president referred to the stance of the three leaders on international courts during a statement that deemed the ICJ’s ruling “unfair.” This would suggest that Myanmar’s implementation of the measures ordered in this judgment, especially its protections on access to citizenship for the Rohingyas, could depend on negotiations shaped by the interests of great powers.
This judgment’s notion of citizenship shows what is really at stake. The ICJ recognized that the denial of citizenship to the Rohingya people was part of a framework of discrimination, which was relevant to its findings on genocidal intent. Nevertheless, it considered granting full and equal citizenship to every Rohingya as “beyond the scope” of appropriate guarantees against another genocide. However, the ICJ did order measures of restitution, including to “ensure the protection of the Rohingya from discrimination and persecution.” The judgment noted in two places that this measure includes “with respect to access to citizenship” and “protection from discrimination in accessing citizenship and with respect to freedom of movement.”
Because the court stopped short of ordering Myanmar to grant citizenship, whether the Rohingya actually receive it will depend on political negotiations in which governments with their own stakes in Myanmar are already engaged. Governments across the world that are in talks with the Myanmar government when it comes to getting access to its territory and resources, from Washington’s interest in rare earths to Beijing’s port at Kyaukphyu and New Delhi’s Kaladan transport corridor, face a crucial choice. They can integrate Rohingya citizenship into the political arrangement, or they can accept the Rohingya’s continued exclusion in order to pursue their own strategic interests. Outside powers should use their leverage, including trade, to make the ruling’s implementation and a long-overdue path to citizenship and safe return part of any settlement they support.
The ICJ delivers its judgment in the case accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority, in The Hague, Netherlands, on November 19, 2026. (REUTERS/Piroschka van de Wouw)
If outside powers back a settlement that leaves the Rohingya stateless, the conditions that drove them from Myanmar will remain, and another exodus will become more likely. In their joint declaration, Judge Leonardo Nemer Caldeira Brant and Judge ad hoc Navi Pillay noted that Myanmar’s obligation to ensure equal access to citizenship should be read into the operative part of the judgment. While recognizing that states have sovereign authority to decide citizenship requirements, they stressed that access to citizenship is necessary for protection and non-recurrence.
Given the current political situation in Myanmar, implementation of this judgment will likely require the cooperation of actors beyond Myanmar’s central government, including the Arakan Army, a nonstate armed group that now controls much of Rakhine State and has also been inflicting abuse on the Rohingyas. Myanmar remains legally responsible for carrying out the restitution ordered by the court and for upholding its obligations under the Genocide Convention, which include preventing and punishing genocide. The court found that Myanmar failed to prevent genocide by civilians acting alongside its security forces, so that duty reaches beyond the state’s own agents. An assurance of safe return from Naypyidaw means little to families going back to townships the Arakan Army controls.
Bangladesh, where more than one million Rohingya refugees now live, seems to have already considered its next diplomatic moves. On November 8, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam talked about engaging with both the Myanmar authorities and the Arakan Army. She raised concerns regarding the wide-ranging opposition in Myanmar to the return of the Rohingyas. This suggests that the Arakan Army’s capture of most of Rakhine from the military, on its own, will not clear the path for the refugees’ return. While the ICJ judgment bolsters the case for a durable return, Dhaka’s negotiations with various actors in Myanmar should continue.
India, too, has interests in Myanmar, in part because of its connectivity ambitions. The port in Sittwe and the Kaladan corridor are part of its Act East strategy to connect the landlocked northeastern states to the Bay of Bengal region. Local businesses are already dealing directly with the Arakan Army, which now holds the territory across the border. On October 31, a Times of India report mentioned a trade agreement between the Siaha district unit of the Mizoram Commercial Vehicles Association and the Arakan Army’s political wing. Indian engagement with Myanmar has been under consideration for a while. As a former Indian ambassador to Myanmar put it last year, “The Chinese openly have relations with all sides; can India afford not to have the same?” Therefore, New Delhi’s reaction to the ICJ judgment appears restrained. While it acknowledged the verdict and supported a sustainable return, it did not use the word genocide.
Citizenship disputes also shape India’s bilateral relations with Bangladesh. After the National Register of Citizens (NRC) exercise left out 1.9 million people from a citizenship registry, the United Nations Refugee Agency warned in September 2019 about the risk of indefinite statelessness. At the time, rights groups warned that it could set off a crisis like the one the Rohingya faced in Myanmar in 2017. The broader geopolitical concern for the region is much about how states distinguish their own citizens from populations they regard as foreign, particularly those communities that are deemed to share ethnic, linguistic, or religious characteristics across the border. Bangladesh has a direct stake in the consequences of this kind of citizenship framing by its two neighbors.
For their part, Chinese policymakers are focused on different kinds of issues when it comes to Myanmar. As Crisis Group has noted, Beijing has long cultivated ties with numerous groups in the country, including the Arakan Army. Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative and Kyaukphyu goals mean that China has an interest in securing a negotiation between armed actors and the Myanmar authorities. Not surprisingly, while Beijing responded to the ICJ judgment with concern regarding judicial overreach, it offered continued support for dialogue. That keeps China positioned as an intermediary without committing it to enforcement, though Beijing is hardly neutral. Crisis Group notes that it threw the military regime a lifeline in 2024. Bangladesh’s challenge is to obtain Chinese backing for repatriation without Beijing treating the Rohingya’s return as something to settle only after its commercial projects are secure.
The role of the United States reflects another set of tensions. While Washington recognized the Myanmar military’s atrocities as genocide in 2022, its current diplomatic priorities appear to have shifted. As Reuters reported earlier this month, a State Department strategy seeks a ceasefire offering a pathway to peace by 2030, through forums on fiscal federalism and territorial demarcation that it links to access to Myanmar’s rare earths. Washington’s reaction to the ICJ verdict laid out concerns for abuses, and at the same time it noted its concern about “politicization” of the court. The question remains as to whether Washington will prioritize citizenship of the Rohingyas or make it a lower priority compared to its commercial opportunities.
Bangladesh has proposed the UN General Assembly as a platform for mobilizing support and building a coalition to press Myanmar and the Arakan Army to carry out the court’s restitution measures, not least since the country now holds the rotating General Assembly presidency. Along its border with Rakhine state, Bangladesh can expand trade as an incentive for further cooperation. Such tools create openings for negotiations. It is crucial that Rohingya representatives and youth participate in such dialogues when it comes to securing full citizenship rights and future repatriations, with the backing of the international community.
Next, the court ruled that Myanmar must report within two years regarding measures it has adopted to provide restitution and, if applicable, compensation. But there is a risk in moving too fast. Negotiations that result in a hurried repatriation that leaves the Rohingya vulnerable could lead to instability, forced exodus, and ultimately additional atrocities. While the ICJ judgment provides Bangladesh and its partners a diplomatic opportunity, international partners must press for a secure Rohingya citizenship status in Myanmar before embarking on future steps.

content:
地方选举前夕，台湾各地候选人进行最后冲刺 - 聚焦台湾
2026 年选举/台湾各地候选人在地方选举前夕进行最后冲刺
要激活文字转语音服务，请首先同意以下隐私政策。
周五，国民党台北市市长蒋万安（左）在凯达格兰大道集会上发表讲话，民进党候选人沉普马（右）则在直播中与支持者会面。 CNA 合成照片 2026 年 11 月 27 日
中新社台北11月27日电 台湾各地的候选人周五在周六的地方选举前加大了竞选力度，举行集会和直播，鼓励选民参加投票，决定谁将领导该国22个市县。
在台北，国民党市长蒋万安在凯达格兰大道上集结支持者，这条大道挤满了人群，一直延伸到总统府外的景福门外。
公布的集会阵容包括立法院院长韩国瑜、台中市长卢秀燕、新北市市长侯友宜、国民党前主席朱立伦、前台北市市长郝龙斌，以及来自台湾另一反对党台湾人民党的嘉宾。
蒋介石于晚上9点20分左右入场。并发表讲话。
值得注意的是，国民党主席郑丽文缺席了宣布的发言阵容，她在蒋介石的连任竞选期间很少与他一起出现。
“由于整体时间和计划的原因，我们必须做出一些选择，”周五早些时候，当被问及她的遗漏时，蒋告诉记者。
蒋介石的挑战者、台湾执政党民进党的沈伯洋，因担心筹备工作造成交通堵塞，取消了两天前计划在仁爱路四段举行的街头集会，随后将选举前夕的活动转移到了网上。
仅在他的竞选活动官方 YouTube 频道上，沉的直播就吸引了超过 330,000 名同时观看的观众。
沉将直播描述为一项“创新”的竞选活动，他说这反映了他开创“民主新时代”的信息。他将竞选期间获得的支持比作支撑他前进的“海浪”。
台湾主要政党领导人在台北以外为其候选人竞选。
总统赖清德（身穿棒球夹克）周五出席新北市长候选人苏巧慧在板桥第二体育场举行的集会。中央通讯社照片2026年11月27日
民进党主席赖清德周五晚上出席新北市长候选人苏巧慧在板桥第二体育场举行的集会。
周五晚上，国民党主席郑女士在竹北市出席了该党新竹县县长候选人徐欣莹的集会。
TPP主席黄国昌也在该市为其党的市长候选人邱臣远竞选。
周五，国民党前主席朱立伦（左）与新北市市长侯裕义（中）在板桥第一体育场集会，为国民党新北市长候选人李树全（右）站台。中央通讯社照片2026年11月27日
在新北，国民党市长候选人李四川在板桥第一体育场安排了一场竞选集会，蒋、陆、侯、韩均是宣布的嘉宾。
蔡还计划出席苏的活动。
桃园市国民党市长张善政举行了长达12小时的直播，结合车队竞选和演播室露面，预计持续至晚上10点。民进党挑战者H

Candidates across Taiwan make final push on eve of local elections - Focus Taiwan
2026 ELECTIONS/Candidates across Taiwan make final push on eve of local elections
To activate the text-to-speech service, please first agree to the privacy policy below.
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (left) of the KMT speaks at a rally on Ketagalan Boulevard while DPP candidate Puma Shen (right) meets supporters on a livestream on Friday. CNA composite photo Nov. 27, 2026
Taipei, Nov. 27 (CNA) Candidates across Taiwan on Friday stepped up campaigning ahead of Saturday's local elections, holding rallies and livestreams to encourage voters to go to the polls in contests that will decide who will lead the country's 22 cities and counties.
In Taipei, Kuomintang (KMT) Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) rallied supporters on Ketagalan Boulevard, which was filled with crowds extending beyond Jingfu Gate outside the Presidential Office.
The rally's announced lineup included Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕), New Taipei Mayor Hou Yu-ih (侯友宜), former KMT Chairman Eric Chu (朱立倫) and former Taipei Mayor Hau Lung-bin (郝龍斌), along with guests from Taiwan's other opposition party, the Taiwan People's Party (TPP).
Chiang made his entrance around 9:20 p.m. and delivered his speech.
Notably absent from the announced speaking lineup was KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文), who has rarely appeared alongside Chiang throughout his reelection campaign.
"Because of the overall timing and program, we had to make some choices," Chiang told reporters earlier Friday when asked about her omission.
Chiang's challenger, Puma Shen (沈伯洋) of Taiwan's ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), moved his election-eve event online after canceling a planned street rally on Renai Road Section 4 two days earlier amid concerns about traffic disruption caused by preparations.
Shen's livestream drew more than concurrent 330,000 viewers on his campaign's official YouTube channel alone.
Describing the livestream as an "innovative" campaign activity, Shen said it reflected his message of ushering in a "new era of democracy." He likened the support he received during his campaign to an "ocean wave" that had kept him going.
The leaders of Taiwan's main political parties campaigned for their candidates outside Taipei.
President Lai Ching-te (in baseball jacket) attends New Taipei mayoral candidate Su Chiao-hui's rally at Banqiao Second Stadium on Friday. CNA photo Nov. 27, 2026
President Lai Ching-te (賴清德), who chairs the DPP, attended New Taipei mayoral candidate Su Chiao-hui's (蘇巧慧) rally at Banqiao Second Stadium on Friday evening.
KMT Chairwoman Cheng attended a rally for her party's Hsinchu County magistrate candidate Hsu Hsin-ying (徐欣瑩) in Zhubei City on Friday evening.
TPP Chairman Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) also campaigned in the city for his party's mayoral candidate, Chiu Chen-yuan (邱臣遠).
Former KMT Chairman Eric Chu (left) and New Taipei Mayor Hou Yu-ih (center) stump for the party's New Taipei mayoral candidate Lee Shu-chuan (right) at Banqiao First Stadium rally on Friday. CNA photo Nov. 27, 2026
In New Taipei, KMT mayoral candidate Lee Shu-chuan (李四川) arranged a rival rally at Banqiao First Stadium, with Chiang, Lu, Hou and Han among the announced guests.
Tsai was also scheduled to appear at Su's event.
Taoyuan's KMT Mayor Chang San-cheng (張善政) held a 12-hour livestream combining motorcade campaigning and studio appearances, scheduled to run until 10 p.m. DPP challenger Huang Shih-chieh (黃世杰) arranged an evening event at the former Federal Tires site in Zhongli District.
Taichung candidates Johnny Chiang (江啟臣) of the KMT and Ho Hsin-chun (何欣純) of the DPP also arranged evening rallies.
In Tainan, the DPP's Chen Ting-fei (陳亭妃) scheduled her final rally for Friday afternoon in Xinying District.
KMT rival Hsieh Lung-chieh (謝龍介) held his major rally Thursday and arranged further street campaigning Friday.
Kaohsiung's DPP candidate Lai Jui-lung (賴瑞隆) chose a site beside Fongshan West MRT Station for his rally, while KMT candidate Ko Chih-en (柯志恩) selected a venue near Dream Mall light rail station.
Besides electing mayors and county magistrates, Saturday's nine-in-one local elections also include contests for council seats and other local elected offices.
Polls open for Taiwan's '9-in-1' elections, nuclear referendum
Polls opened across Taiwan at 8 a.m. Saturday for the "9-in-1" local elections and a referendum on nuclear power, with voters choosing local government leaders and representatives and deciding whether to abolish the country's nuclear-free energy policy.
Candidates, party leaders step up campaigning ahead of Saturday's elections
With two days to go before Saturday's elections, New Taipei mayoral candidates stepped up campaigning Thursday, with the Kuomintang's (KMT) Lee Shu-chuan (李四川) making his 100th market visit of the campaign and the Democratic Progressive Party's (DPP) Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧) campaigning by motorcade through seven districts.
Taipei mayor candidates cancel rallies amid road use controversy
The leading candidates for Taipei mayor have canceled major in-person political rallies amid a dispute over road usage rights, just days before Taiwan's local elections on Saturday.

2025 年 9 月，位于弗吉尼亚州阿灵顿的五角大楼。（亚历克斯·布兰登/美联社）
三名知情人士告诉路透社，黑客已经攻破了美国空军的旗舰云计算平台，这一进展可能会危及大量敏感的战术、人员和后勤数据。
两名知情人士表示，Cloud One 的入侵是在过去一个月左右的系统升级工作中发现的，并补充说这一发现导致了整个平台的中断。路透社无法确定黑客的身份、入侵的全部范围或是否有任何数据被盗。
美国空军在给路透社的一份声明中表示，“不会对特定网络和系统的安全态势、漏洞或运行状态发表评论。我们不断采取审慎措施来保护（空军）部门的信息、系统和任务能力。”
Cloud One 于 2017 年启动，旨在成为满足空军 IT 需求的一站式商店，结合了微软、亚马逊、甲骨文和 Alphabet 四大运营商的资源，为数十种应用程序提供支持，包括管理人员数据和薪酬或后勤和维护的应用程序。
其中包括空军的基于云的指挥与控制系统，该系统会整理来自北美各地的防空雷达和其他数据源，以及战区综合作战弹药系统，该系统会跟踪全球 200 多个美国空军基地的炸弹和导弹。
SAIC 一直是 Cloud One 的主承包商，直到 2025 年 Leidos 接手。国家工商总局没有回应置评请求。莱多斯将问题转交给空军。
据两位消息人士称，Cloud One 是美国军方最大的云平台之一。
“这里的违规行为是一件大事，”一位消息人士说。
其中一位消息人士称，调查人员已请美国军方的网络部队网络司令部来评估损失。
网络司令部没有回应置评请求。
黑客事件的发现导致了一系列的破坏。其中两名消息人士和第四名知情人士表示，将后台应用程序迁移到云一的努力已经暂停，这是一项长期的军事优先事项。
就在科技行业披露了新一批严重软件漏洞之际，云一号上已经运行的应用程序的更新被阻止，导致空军人员无法应用修复程序。第五位消息人士称，一些用户的管理员权限被撤销。
所有五位消息人士均要求匿名。
一位消息人士称，网络入侵者利用软件漏洞到达控制平面。该人士将控制飞机比作通用遥控器，因为理论上入侵者可以利用其访问权限来检查军用飞机的运行状态或备件的移动情况，尽管目前尚不清楚黑客在这种情况下是否这样做。
路透社无法识别具体情况

Hackers breach US Air Force flagship Cloud One computing platform
Mike Stone and Raphael Satter, Reuters

The Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, September 2025. (Alex Brandon/AP)
Hackers have breached the U.S. Air Force’s flagship cloud computing platform, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters, in a development that could jeopardize a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.
The intrusion at Cloud One was discovered within the past month or so during work to upgrade the system, two of the people said, adding that the discovery has led to disruption across the platform. Reuters could not establish the identity of the hackers, the full scope of the intrusion or whether any data had been stolen.
In a statement to Reuters, the Air Force said it “does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the Air Force) information, systems and mission capabilities.”
Initiated in 2017, Cloud One was meant to serve as a one-stop shop for the Air Force’s IT needs, combining the resources of four operators — Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet — to power scores of applications including ones that manage personnel data and pay or logistics and maintenance.
Among them are the Air Force’s Cloud-Based Command and Control, which collates air defense radar and other data feeds from across North America, and the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System, which tracks bombs and missiles across more than 200 U.S. Air Force locations around the world.
SAIC was the prime contractor for Cloud One until 2025, when Leidos took over. SAIC did not respond to a request seeking comment. Leidos referred questions to the Air Force.
Cloud One is among the U.S. military’s biggest cloud platforms, according to two of the sources.
“A breach here is a big deal,” one of the sources said.
Investigators have called in Cyber Command, the U.S. military’s cyber force, to assess the damage, one of the sources said.
Cyber Command did not respond to requests for comment.
The discovery of the hack led to a range of disruption. Two of the sources, along with a fourth person familiar with the matter, said that efforts to migrate back-office applications to Cloud One, a longstanding military priority, have been paused.
Updates to applications already running on Cloud One were blocked, leaving Air Force personnel unable to apply fixes just as a new batch of serious software vulnerabilities has been disclosed across the technology industry. A fifth source said that some users had their administrator rights revoked.
All five sources spoke on condition of anonymity.
One source said that the cyber intruders exploited a software vulnerability to reach the control plane. That person likened the control plane to a universal remote, as intruders in theory could leverage their access to check the operational status of military aircraft or the movement of spare parts, though it was unclear whether the hackers did so in this case.
Reuters could not identify the specific vulnerability exploited by the hackers.
News of the breach comes amid heightened anxiety over AI-powered intrusions, a particularly serious problem for cloud-based networks because of the ability of AI models to swiftly detect weaknesses across wide surface areas.
The U.S. government already has been dealing with the fallout from at least six other recently disclosed cyber incidents, including two at the FBI, a previous hack of Pentagon data, a recent leak of Department of Homeland Security personnel information, a breach affecting at least two spy agencies and a hack at the Treasury Department.
Cloud One has long been in the crosshairs of hackers.
In a 2023 commentary carried by the online publication FedScoop, Cloud One’s leadership touted what they called a “100% success rate” in beating back what they said was a “staggering” number of attempts to penetrate the platform.
“There is no room for error when it comes to security,” Cloud One’s leadership wrote.
Mike Stone and Raphael Satter, Reuters

周五在中共人口战略指挥部会议上起草的草案还包括大规模减税以支持生育和育儿，以及设立人口战略机构，负责相关措施。
总部负责人、前自民党政策负责人下村博文在会后对记者表示：“我想传达一个信息，让人们相信政府是认真对待让整个社会支持育儿的想法的。”
他提出了将具体措施纳入政府《2027年经济财政管理和改革基本方针》的计划。
草案提出了减缓人口下降速度、建设适应人口减少社会的基本方针，要求扩大免费托儿服务的资格年龄，支持生育治疗。
另一个建议是通过促进多样化的工作方式来增加空闲时间，例如缩短正式员工每天的工作时间，以便在面临劳动力短缺的社会中保持社会经济活力。此外，敦促政府将老年人的年龄从目前的65岁或以上提高，并修改工作年龄人口的定义，目前工作年龄人口是指15岁至64岁之间的人。
此外，草案还要求将一些都道府县指定为应对人口下降的特别措施区。报告称：“不应无限制地接受外国工人，而应在维持社会经济活动所需的范围内接受外国工人。”
会议上，有人呼吁减轻高等教育财政负担。
这些提案预计将于下周在经过党内程序后提交给首相高市早苗。

LDP proposes ¥10 million benefits for third and subsequent children
The ruling Liberal Democratic Party's draft set of proposals, including the distribution of ¥10 million benefits each for third and subsequent children, are part of a population strategy the government plans to formulate by the year-end. | REUTERS
X Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Bluesky Threads Email Print Bookmark story Copy link
The ruling Liberal Democratic Party has drawn up a draft set of proposals including the distribution of ¥10 million benefits each for third and subsequent children as part of a population strategy the government plans to formulate by year-end.
The draft, compiled at a meeting of the party’s population strategy headquarters Friday, also includes large-scale tax reductions to support childbirth and child-rearing, and the establishment of a population strategy agency, which would be in charge of related measures.
“I want to issue a message convincing people that the government is serious about the idea of letting the entire society support child-rearing,” Hakubun Shimomura, chief of the headquarters and former LDP policy head, told reporters after the meeting.
He showed a plan to incorporate concrete measures into the government’s Basic Policy on Economic and Fiscal Management and Reform for 2027.
The draft sets basic policies of slowing the pace of population decline and creating a society adapted to a decreasing population, calling for expanding eligibility age for free nursery services and support for fertility treatment.
Another suggestion is to increase free time by promoting diverse work styles, such as regular employees who work shorter hours a day, in order to maintain socioeconomic vitality in a society facing labor shortages. In addition, the government would be urged to raise the age defining people as elderly from the current 65 or older and revise the definition of the working-age population, which currently refers to people between the ages of 15 and 64.
Furthermore, the draft calls for designating some prefectures as special measures zones to counter population declines. “Foreign workers should not be accepted without limits but should be accepted to the extent necessary to maintain socioeconomic activities,” it says.
At the meeting, there were calls for reducing the financial burden of higher education.
The proposals are expected to be handed to Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi next week after intraparty procedures.

zh_title: 立陶宛发出警告，台湾排除更改办公室名称的可能
summary: 台湾在立陶宛警告中排除办公室更名的可能性 - 焦点台湾 台湾在立陶宛警告中排除办公室更名的可能性 要激活文本转语音服务，请首先同意以下隐私政策。台湾驻立陶宛代表处。中新社台北11月27日电 (中央社)外交部周五表示，台湾没有计划更名驻立陶宛代表处。在立陶宛领导人警告可能单方面改变驻立陶宛代表处地位后，台湾呼吁相互尊重。该办事处目前名为“台湾办事处”
content:
立陶宛发出警告，台湾排除更改办公室名称的可能 - 焦点台湾
立陶宛发出警告，台湾排除更改办公室名称的可能
要激活文字转语音服务，请首先同意以下隐私政策。
台湾驻立陶宛代表处。 CNA档案照片
中新社台北11月27日电 在立陶宛领导人警告可能单方面改变驻立陶宛代表处地位后，外交部周五表示，台湾没有计划更名驻立陶宛代表处，并呼吁相互尊重。
该办事处目前称为台湾驻立陶宛代表处。
它于 2021 年 11 月开业，成为台湾在欧洲首个使用“台湾”而非惯用“台北”名称的代表处。北京的回应是降级外交关系并限制双边贸易。
外交部在一份声明中表示，两国政府经过认真协商后同意了这个名称，反映了两国共同的民主价值观和加强双边关系的愿望。
“真诚和相互尊重是双边关系的基石，”外交部表示，并补充说，双方应尊重现有共识，维护已经建立的合作和信任。
外交部将台湾和立陶宛称为前线民主国家，敦促两国共同反对威权扩张和分裂民主国家的努力。
在此声明之前，立陶宛总理明道加斯·辛克维丘斯和总统吉塔纳斯·瑙塞达表示，立陶宛在寻求恢复与中国的关系时可以单方面改变该办事处的法律地位。
据立陶宛公共广播公司 LRT 报道，辛克维丘斯周三在接受 ELTA 通讯社采访时表示，如果台湾拒绝更改其名称，立陶宛可能会撤销该办事处的法律地位。
他指出，政府已通过部长令授予该办公室认证，其未来地位由政府决定。
“我们不希望这样，但可以使用这个选项，”他说。
然而，根据立陶宛新闻网站 TV3.lt 刊登的 ELTA 报道，辛克维丘斯周四强调，撤销该办公室的认证并不是政府的目标。
他说，授予认可的当局也可以撤销认可，但立陶宛正在寻求一项安排，使其能够与台湾和中国保持关系。
据轻快铁报道，瑙塞达周四表示，这个问题可以通过共同协议或单方面行动来解决，同时强调保持与台湾关系的重要性。
“近年来的期望是一回事，但实际结果是另一回事，”他在布鲁塞尔对记者表示，并称台湾投资不足。
两位领导人都没有宣布决定，也没有在讲话中设定单方面行动的最后期限。
立陶宛议会外交事务委员会主席雷米吉尤斯·莫图扎斯周四对轻轨电台表示，关闭办事处并不是目标。
前总理英格丽达·西蒙尼特 (Ingrida Šimonytė) 在接受同一家广播公司采访时批评了她所说的对北京的先发制人的让步，认为仅根据经济利益来判断与台湾的关系是肤浅的。
台湾此前曾通过外交部副部长陈明琪的讲话排除了11月10日更名的可能性。

【原文 English Original】
Taiwan rules out office name change amid Lithuanian warning - Focus Taiwan
Taiwan rules out office name change amid Lithuanian warning
To activate the text-to-speech service, please first agree to the privacy policy below.
The Taiwanese Representative Office in Lithuania. CNA file photo
Taipei, Nov. 27 (CNA) Taiwan has no plans to rename its representative office in Lithuania, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) said Friday, calling for mutual respect after Lithuanian leaders warned of the possibility of unilaterally changing the office's status.
The office is currently known as The Taiwanese Representative Office in Lithuania.
It opened in November 2021, becoming Taiwan's first representative office in Europe to use "Taiwanese" rather than the customary "Taipei" designation. Beijing responded by downgrading diplomatic relations and restricting bilateral trade.
The two governments agreed on the name after careful consultation, reflecting their shared democratic values and desire to strengthen bilateral relations, MOFA said in a statement.
"Good faith and mutual respect are the cornerstones of bilateral relations," the ministry said, adding that both sides should honor their existing consensus and preserve the cooperation and trust they have built.
Describing Taiwan and Lithuania as frontline democracies, MOFA urged the two countries to stand together against authoritarian expansion and efforts to divide democracies.
The statement followed remarks by Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius and President Gitanas Nausėda that Lithuania could unilaterally change the office's legal status as it seeks to restore relations with China.
In an interview with news agency ELTA on Wednesday, Sinkevičius said Lithuania could revoke the office's legal status if Taiwan refused to change its name, according to Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT.
He noted that the government had granted the office accreditation through a ministerial order and its future status was for the government to decide.
"We would not want that, but this option could be used," he said.
On Thursday, however, Sinkevičius stressed that withdrawing the office's accreditation was not the government's objective, according to an ELTA report carried by Lithuanian news website TV3.lt.
He said authorities that grant accreditation could also withdraw it, but that Lithuania was seeking an arrangement that would allow it to maintain relations with both Taiwan and China.
Nausėda said Thursday that the issue could be handled through mutual agreement or unilateral action, while emphasizing the importance of preserving ties with Taiwan, LRT reported.
"Expectations in recent years were one thing, but the actual outcome was another," he told reporters in Brussels, describing Taiwanese investment as insufficient.
Neither leader announced a decision or set a deadline for unilateral action in their remarks.
Lithuanian parliamentary Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Remigijus Motuzas told LRT radio Thursday that closing the office was not the objective.
Speaking to the same broadcaster, former Prime Minister Ingrida Šimonytė criticized what she described as preemptive concessions to Beijing, arguing that judging ties with Taiwan solely by their economic benefits was superficial.
Taiwan had previously ruled out a name change on Nov. 10, through remarks by Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi (陳明祺).
Talks on an investment action plan proposed by Lithuania in March were suspended during the country's political transition in June but resumed in July, MOFA previously said.
In April, the ministry said Taiwan had invested more than 16.8 million euros in Lithuania since 2021.
In February, then-Prime Minister Inga Ruginienė said Lithuania had "jumped in front of a train and lost," arguing that the decision on the office's name had not been coordinated with the European Union or the United States.

title: Dispatch from 2032: After Chinese salvos fail to defeat Taiwan, Beijing is trapped in a war of attrition
zh_title: 2032年快讯：中国联军未能击败台湾，北京陷入消耗战
summary: 2032 年快讯：中国齐射未能击败台湾后，北京陷入消耗战 - 大西洋理事会的军舰和中国人民解放军 (PLA) 海军战斗机于 2018 年 4 月 12 日在南海参加军事展示。（路透社/斯金格，来自Reuters Connect）本文是斯考克罗夫特中心的系列文章“来自下一场战争的快讯”的一部分印度-太平洋安全倡议，其中我们的专家对世界下一场重大冲突在最有可能爆发的地区可能会是什么样子进行了假设：
content:
2032年快讯：中国的齐射未能击败台湾，北京陷入消耗战 - 大西洋理事会
2018 年 4 月 12 日，中国人民解放军 (PLA) 海军的军舰和战斗机参加在南海举行的军事展示。（路透社/斯金格，来自Reuters Connect）
本文是斯考克罗夫特中心印度-太平洋安全倡议系列“下一场战争的快报”的一部分，其中我们的专家对世界下一场重大冲突可能在最有可能爆发的地区印度-太平洋地区进行了假设。这些消息被称为虚构情报，或“FicInt”，在军队内部使用，让政策制定者为可能的未来做好准备。目的是防止下一场战争爆发。
2032 年，台北——中国第一批导弹和无人机在夜深人静时飞越台湾海峡。有些在咆哮的火焰喷射的推动下划过黑色的天空，而另一些则安静地、几乎看不见地以稳定的速度在黑暗的天空中嗡嗡作响。第一个被拦截导弹击中中国火柱摧毁，其他则在被激光闪光击中时爆炸。有些被小型拦截无人机撞到一边。一些人被自动炮和机枪的火幕击落，曳光弹在黑暗中摸索着目标，越来越多的条纹。
这些联合火力打击——中国对台战争中所宣称的第一次攻击——旨在摧毁台湾的防御，使其军事力量丧失能力，并粉碎台湾人的战斗意志。尽管这些齐射令人恐惧且令人印象深刻，但它们未能实现中国的目标。
一些袭击成功了，坠入港口、机场和军事基地，并向天空喷出滚滚火焰和浓烟。北起台北，南至高雄，台湾一次又一次遭到无情的打击。虽然台湾军事力量的来源是中国的目标，但许多平民也因这次袭击而被屠杀。世界领导人最初等着看台湾是否能够承受住这场冲击，或者是否会像许多分析人士预测的那样迅速崩溃。
但事实证明，台湾的多层防空和导弹防御系统“T-Dome”出乎意料地有效。尽管该公司在 2027 年首次投入运营时（即 2025 年宣布成立两年后）面临性能困难，但其许多自主系统的可靠性迅速成熟。随着中国入侵台湾领空和侵略性海上骚扰的行为年复一年变得更加频繁和充满敌意，台湾的总统和指挥官们更加放心地相信T-Dome允许自主攻击其认定的敌对目标。
尽管中国在发动袭击之前发起了旨在破坏台湾指挥和控制系统的强大网络攻势，但台湾慷慨地使用了 Anthropic 的 Claude Mythos 等前沿人工智能 (AI) 网络安全模型，发现并修补了几乎所有潜在的攻击向量，从而保持了 T-Dome 和其他系统的运行。对人工智能抱有如此大的信心的争议是不可避免的。战时的防御效果则不然。
T-Dome 证明了这些高风险决策的正确性，在第一轮拦截中拦截了 90% 的中国弹药。这为台湾指挥官赢得了宝贵的时间来分散兵力，使中国更难瞄准他们，采取预先计划

【原文 English Original】
Dispatch from 2032: After Chinese salvos fail to defeat Taiwan, Beijing is trapped in a war of attrition - Atlantic Council
Warships and fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Navy take part in a military display in the South China Sea on April 12, 2018. (REUTERS/Stringer via Reuters Connect)
This article is part of “Dispatches from the Next War,” a series from the Scowcroft Center’s Indo-Pacific Security Initiative in which our experts provide hypothetical accounts of what the world’s next major conflict could look like in the region where it’s most likely to break out: the Indo-Pacific. These dispatches are styled as fictional intelligence, or “FicInt,” which is used within the military to prepare policymakers for possible futures. The aim is to prevent the next war from ever unfolding.
TAIPEI, 2032—China’s first missiles and drones flew across the Taiwan Strait in the dead of night. Some coursed across the black sky propelled by growling jets of flame, while others quietly and near-invisibly hummed through the dark sky at a steady pace. The first were destroyed by interceptor missiles snaking into Chinese columns of fire, others exploded when hit by flashes of laser light. Some were knocked aside by tiny interceptor drones. A few were downed by curtains of autocannon and machine-gun fire, with the growing streaks of tracer bullets groping for targets in the dark.
These joint firepower strikes—the vaunted first attack of China’s war on Taiwan—were meant to smash Taiwan’s defenses, incapacitate its military force, and shatter the Taiwanese will to fight. While these salvoes were terrifying and impressive, they failed to achieve China’s objectives.
Some of the attacks got through, crashing into ports, airfields, and military bases, and sending plumes of flame and smoke into the sky. From Taipei in the north to Kaohsiung in the south, Taiwan was mercilessly hit again and again. While sources of Taiwanese military power were China’s target, many civilians were also slaughtered by the attack. World leaders initially waited to see whether Taiwan could withstand the onslaught or whether it would quickly fold as many analysts had predicted.
But the T-Dome, Taiwan’s multi-layered air- and missile-defense system, proved unexpectedly effective. While it faced performance difficulties when it first became operational in 2027, two years after its announcement in 2025, the reliability of many of its autonomous systems matured rapidly. As China’s incursions into Taiwan’s airspace and aggressive maritime harassment grew more frequent and hostile year after year, Taiwan’s presidents and commanders became more comfortable putting greater faith in the T-Dome’s permission to autonomously engage targets it identified as hostile.
And while China’s strikes were preceded by a robust cyber offensive aimed at disrupting Taiwan’s command-and-control systems, Taiwan’s generous use of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) cybersecurity models like Anthropic’s Claude Mythos had discovered and patched nearly every potential attack vector, keeping the T-Dome and other systems operational. The controversy about placing so much faith in AI was inevitable; the defensive results in wartime were not.
The T-Dome vindicated those high-risk decisions, intercepting 90 percent of Chinese munitions in the first barrage. This bought Taiwan’s commanders precious time to disperse their forces and make it more difficult for China to target them, take up preplanned fighting positions across their nation, and start fighting back.
Further, the survivability and resilience of many Taiwanese bases, stations, and command posts proved to be highly robust. Many were built underground and were well-protected by dozens of meters of earth and rock. Missile after missile and drone after drone slammed into the vicinity of these underground command posts. While some were disrupted, as antennas were toppled and wiring cut, most remained operational.
Notably, Taiwan’s air force was able to maintain aviation command and control from its underground airbase within Toad Mountain, contributing both to air defense and strike missions of its own. Above-ground targets in Taiwan, such as airfields and main supply routes, were initially cratered and some aircraft were destroyed. But Taiwanese engineers repaired airfields, roads, and bases with alacrity. As a result, such hits resulted only in temporary pauses in Taiwan’s operations and did not amount to debilitating knock-out blows.
With most of its forces intact, Taiwan counter-attacked, firing its own munitions at key targets across mainland China. Many of these were intercepted. But due to the superior quality and reliability of Taiwan’s munitions, and China’s years-long strategic emphasis on offensive rather than defensive capabilities, a disproportionate number of Taiwanese munitions hit their marks.
In addition, the United States, Japan, and other nations provided Taiwan with exquisite intelligence and provided non-attributable, non-kinetic cyber and space capabilities that greatly enhanced the hit-rate of Taiwan’s defensive counterstrikes. Consequently, Taiwan devastated targets such as the ports where China’s amphibious forces were assembling, crippling the invasion before it even got underway. Chinese aviation command-and-control nodes and over-the-horizon radars were also hammered, giving Taiwan’s air force greater freedom of maneuver than most analysts had ever predicted.
The effects on Taiwanese morale were immeasurable. As with the US military’s famous Doolittle Raid on Japan after Pearl Harbor, the physical damage Taiwan inflicted on China was less important than the political and psychological results of Taiwan’s demonstrated resilience. Taiwan was not helpless, and the People’s Republic of China was not an invincible juggernaut.
With the quick, decisive campaign China had envisioned to isolate and invade Taiwan thwarted, the joint firepower strikes pressed on. Days dragged into weeks. Taiwan began running dry on interceptors, cannons began to jam, and even lasers began to burn out. Taiwan was forced to absorb more direct hits from Chinese strikes, even as China’s own magazines ran low.
If the war were evaluated today based on targets hit, the assessment would find that China has a commanding lead. But even with Taiwan’s dwindling munitions, the forces still in the fight have proven disproportionately effective. As the United States painfully experienced during Operation Epic Fury in Iran, even a greatly diminished adversary can still hold the advantage if it fights asymmetrically and selectively. While short on missiles, Taiwan has maintained plenty of launchers and conducted carefully sequenced strikes layered with joint operations and allied intelligence support that continue to bloody China’s nose. China’s Eastern Theater Command has still refused to launch an invasion fleet across the strait, as the mere preservation of Taiwan’s stand-in forces held the amphibious force at risk, making the amphibious invasion appear infeasible.
China—and the world—also grossly underestimated Taiwanese resolve. Despite polling that showed Taiwanese willingness to fight as even higher than that of Ukrainians prior to the Russian invasion in 2022, many analysts were skeptical that Taiwan would hold fast under the pressure of a Chinese offensive. Such analysts had focused primarily on the correlation of forces and means between China and Taiwan, weighing their assessments on numeric comparisons of ships, jets, and missiles available to both sides. This, however, failed to account for qualitative differences in Chinese and Taiwanese systems and societies, or for fundamental human elements that have always characterized the conduct of war. While bombing alone was not China’s plan, China had been as yet unable to launch its amphibious invasion because it could not set the necessary conditions. Bombing alone has never produced capitulation, and it has not here in Taipei.
Moreover, China’s narrative warfare and United Front activities, its strategic co-opting of domestic groups, had also penetrated swaths of Taiwanese society and foreign discourse, influencing pre-war public commentary to give a dim view of Taiwanese will and an overinflated view of Chinese prowess. The extreme pro-unification wing of the Kuomintang, the Chinese Nationalist Party in Taiwan, aligned itself with Beijing before the war. A few American commentators had advocated strategic restraint, isolationism, and nativism, while some American politicians echoed these sentiments, leading many to presume Taiwan would surrender at the first blush with its enemy.
But as with the staunch resolve of Ukrainians, it appears the Taiwanese are prepared to fight for years if necessary to preserve the democracy and way of life they built after ending martial law in 1987. Under attack, as they have seen their people killed in the streets, the Taiwanese have bravely rallied, pro-unification extremists have been politically isolated, and public sentiment in favor of taidu, formal Taiwanese independence, has skyrocketed. Civil-defense initiatives and energy-diversification efforts, which had been maturing for years, have also mentally prepared the population and the entire society to be resilient despite the immediate imposition of incredible hardship across the country.
Beijing now faces a dilemma. Backing down could deal a fatal blow to the credibility of the Chinese Communist Party, while pressing on would mean doubling down on sunk costs and putting the government’s dream of national rejuvenation further out of reach. Caught in a trap of its own making, China has looked abroad to Russia and North Korea for other solutions, while the Central Military Commission has begun to consider limited nuclear strikes to turn the tide in China’s favor.
Magazine depth cuts both ways. Taiwan may run low on munitions first in a future conflict, but even Chinese inventories are not limitless. And because China cannot hit everything at once, it will likely have to focus on high-priority targets, yielding maneuver space for Taiwanese forces.
Range rings also cut both ways. Taiwan falls within the range of most Chinese strike capabilities. China, too, is within range of many of Taiwan’s strike capabilities. If Taiwan is attacked by China, Taiwan will strike back at targets in China—not just at munitions or forces entering Taiwanese territory.
The earth is the most reliable and affordable shield. Interceptors are necessary, but they can be expensive and can quickly run dry under constant barrage. While difficult to scale, subterranean fortifications reduce reliance on interceptors and mitigate China’s ability to effectively target Taiwan’s forces.
Regardless of when, why, and how China may start the fight, the result would likely be a protracted war with Taiwan. Beijing may intend—and pundits may predict—a quick surrender by Taipei, but this is unlikely. There are many “roads to war” and rationales Beijing will claim led to its aggression, and many ways the war might begin, including a quarantine, a blockade, or outright attack. Regardless, China is unlikely to win rapidly or easily, almost inevitably leading to a protracted and costly conflict—if Taiwan continues its defense and resilience efforts.
Even successful strikes rarely deliver knockout blows, and an active defense can prove resilient even under sustained strike campaigns. Defenders will disperse to preserve forces and capabilities, and can rapidly repair airfields, ports, and bases.
When nations are attacked, cohesion surges, even among politically divided states. Blood calls for blood, defenders rally to their flag, and the will to fight becomes stronger than ever.
Third parties are not easily intimidated into total non-participation in wars that impact them. When nations can pursue their interests and frustrate their adversaries at low risk, they will.

title: 英伟达先进晶片安装在与黄仁勋外遇对象有关联的中国数据中心
summary: 英伟达Blackwell晶片安装在与黄仁勋外遇对象有关联的中国数据中心。图为中天新闻网提供的视频截屏显示，中国女商人黄乐（Alice Huang）今年5月出席美国科技巨企英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋（黑衣者）在台北主办的晚宴。 （法新社） 美国科技巨企英伟达的先进Blackwell晶片，被安装在与英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋外遇对象有关联的中国数据中心。 据彭博社报道，两家中国公司在上海一座与黄仁勋外遇对象黄乐（Alice Huang）有关联的数据中心，安装了英伟达性能强大的Blackw
content:
英伟达Blackwell晶片安装在与黄仁勋外遇对象有关联的中国数据中心。图为中天新闻网提供的视频截屏显示，中国女商人黄乐（Alice Huang）今年5月出席美国科技巨企英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋（黑衣者）在台北主办的晚宴。 （法新社）
美国科技巨企英伟达的先进Blackwell晶片，被安装在与英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋外遇对象有关联的中国数据中心。
据彭博社报道，两家中国公司在上海一座与黄仁勋外遇对象黄乐（Alice Huang）有关联的数据中心，安装了英伟达性能强大的Blackwell晶片。
根据11月向中国监管机构提交文件所列明的序列号，安装在长三角项目的设备包括一套GB300 NVL72机架系统，这是英伟达性能最强大的产品之一。
彭博社查阅的贷款机构文件显示，上海硕曜科技以这些硬件作为抵押，从上海科创银行获得9600万元人民币（1861万新元）贷款。
总部设于东京的上海科栈科技在上述数据中心安装的一台GB200服务器，也采用Blackwell晶片。根据上述提交文件，上海科栈科技在2025年底从一家由上海当地政府机构全资拥有的融资租赁公司获得9000万元人民币贷款。
这些文件首次揭示，英伟达Blackwell处理器流入了一座与黄乐和总部设在新加坡的云计算与人工智能算力服务商超速国际有关联的中国数据中心。直到不久前，这些处理器还是英伟达性能最强大的数据中心产品，而且在没有获得美国许可的情况下，向中国出口这类产品一直都是非法的。
美国总统特朗普曾明确表示，至少目前他不希望这些晶片流向中国。OpenAI和Anthropic PBC使用这类晶片训练旗下最先进的模型。
与此同时，英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋曾声称，这些设备体积太大，不容易跨境走私：一套标准的两米高GB300 NVL72服务器机架内含72颗Blackwell Ultra晶片和36颗Grace处理器，重量可超过1500公斤，体积相当于一台巨型冰箱。
目前尚不清楚这套GB300机架是如何进入中国、如何到了上海硕曜科技手中，又是如何进入上述特定场所。当地媒体称，该场所的设计容量最高可容纳80万台服务器。
彭博将该产品的序列号输入一个公开的保修数据库后发现，这套设备由台湾的技嘉科技制造。技嘉将英伟达晶片组装成服务器和机架。该数据库还提供了与这一序列号对应的型号名称，与这家台湾公司生产的一款GB300 NVL72服务器机架相符。
这类设备在安装到数据中心之前，往往会经过多方之手，其中包括当地的分销网络。在许多情况下，最终被走私进入中国的产品，最初是出售给不受限制地区的买家。
彭博向技嘉提供了这套机架的序列号，并询问技嘉最初将这套硬件出售给了谁以及出售时间。技嘉以公司政策为由拒绝回答这些问题。公司发言人在电邮声明中表示，该公司“开展所有业务时均遵守适用的法律法规。所有交易均须遵守我们的内部合规要求以及交易当时有效的相关法律法规。”
采购这套GB300机架并将其用作抵押品的上海硕曜科技，在与黄乐有关联的上述数据中心开展业务，同时与超速国际存在显著交集。彭博社此前报道，由于担忧超速国际将英伟达晶片走私至中国，超速国际正受到美国调查。
过去一年，上海硕曜科技一直未回应彭博询问，但本月在一份罕见的公开声明中证实，该公司是超速国际的服务提供商之一，并称双方关系“仅限于普通商业合作”。
与此同时，超速国际在2024年向投资者介绍其最大的数据中心时，使用了长三角项目的效果图，并将这一场所称为位于某个未具名国家的“特定区域”设施。
彭博没有证据表明超速国际本身曾将英伟达硬件转流至上述地点。对于美国的调查，超速国际也否认存在不当行为。该公司一直没有回答有关长三角项目的多次询问。英伟达同样没有回应。多年来，英伟达一直坚称其产品不存在黑市，也未回应针对此篇报道提出的问题。
特朗普政府本月将超速国际列入美国贸易黑名单，理由是该公司存在参与晶片转流活动的重大风险。

content:
大陸額人氣男星張凌赫資料照。（Kate Green/Getty Images for Gucci）
【大紀元2026年11月28日訊】（大紀元記者佟亦加報導）大陸人氣男星張凌赫與女星田曦薇憑藉古裝劇《逐玉》俘獲大批粉絲，兩人上週舉辦線上粉絲見面會時不僅大讚台灣美食，而且張凌赫還隔空喊話表示「非常想去台灣」與粉絲見面。對此，陸委會副主委梁文傑回應，觀察張凌赫是積極配合中共統戰，台灣方面說不。
因古裝劇《逐玉》爆紅的張凌赫，今年10月曾傳出來台舉辦粉絲見面會。陸委會10月21日回應，歡迎中國藝人來台交流，但不能帶有統戰色彩。
張凌赫過去多次在個人微博轉發配合中共官方定調的帖文，包含「中國台灣省」、「台灣從來不是一個國家」以及「國土不可分」等言論，中共又刻意安排他今年6月在「海峽論壇」演講，因此拒絕他來台交流。
沒想到，張凌赫與《逐玉》同劇女主田曦薇上週末舉行線上粉絲見面會，吸引超過26萬人次觀看。兩人在線上繼續表達盼望能來台交流的願望，且「中共中央國家安全委員會辦公室」隨後也喊話，希望台灣不要阻撓兩岸影視交流。
對此，陸委會副主委梁文傑11月26日回應，上次張凌赫申請來台時已作說明，表示會觀察張凌赫日後行為。不過觀察過後發現，張凌赫不是單純被迫配合，而是積極主動配合中共統戰單位的一些活動。
梁文傑說，他當時留下「青山綠水，有緣還能再見」的說法，暗示張凌赫若停止配合統戰宣傳，未來仍有機會獲准來台。
但沒過多久，中共《新華社》11月13日發布一篇題為「解決台灣問題、實現祖國完全統一」的政治宣傳文章，張凌赫不僅隨即在微博轉發原文，並寫下「國土不可分國家不可亂，民族不可散文明不可斷」等配文，直接踩到陸委會觀察期的紅線。
陸委會認定張凌赫是基於自身市場利益，積極主動配合中共統戰任務。因此梁文傑直言，張凌赫「又配合中共發文，所以就算想要再見他，也沒有可能」，表示這是張凌赫自己的選擇。
梁文傑強調：「我們歡迎兩岸藝人的交流，但是如果這位藝人來台是兼統戰任務、有統戰色彩的話，我們當然會Say No。」
針對張凌赫無法來台，中共國台辦發言人25日辯稱是「民進黨當局」處心積慮阻撓兩岸民眾交流往來。但陸委會反駁說，中共經常刻意操作，將單純交流活動沾染政治宣傳目的，才是阻撓兩岸正常有序交流的元凶。

content:
菲律宾武装部队2024年6月17日发布的视频截图照片显示，中国海岸警卫队成员在南中国海第二托马斯沙洲（中国称为仁爱礁）附近冲撞菲律宾海岸警卫队船只并发生暴力冲突。
菲律宾国防部星期五(11月27日)表示，中国“无权也无道德基础”指使菲律宾如何选择防务伙伴。在此之前，中国国防部谴责菲律宾与澳大利亚近日签署的防务协议，并称菲律宾的“个别政客”“妄图拉拢域外国家”插手南中国海问题。
菲律宾国防部发言人阿塞尼奥·安多隆(Arsenio Andolong)在一份声明中表示：“中国既无权也无道德基础指使菲律宾如何以及与谁合作来捍卫国家主权和利益。”
他补充道：“我们与其他国家的关系，尤其是在国防和安全问题上，不需要北京的许可。”
安多隆指责正是北京，而不是像北京所说的其他国家，加剧了地区紧张局势。
他说：“中国对其他国家挑起紧张局势的虚假指责太过了，与此同时，它仍在继续使用胁迫、恐吓和武力来维护其在西菲律宾海和其他水域的非法主张。”
西菲律宾海是菲律宾政府对菲律宾群岛以西、属于其主张的装束经济区内的部分南中国海海域的称呼。中国宣称对南中国海拥有几乎全部的主权。除了中国和菲律宾外，越南、马来西亚、文莱和台湾也主张对南中国海拥有几乎全部或部分主权。目前南中国海局势大体上平静，但是中国与菲律宾在南中国海争议海域的对峙和对抗却有愈演愈烈之势。
安多隆敦促中国停止恐吓行为，尊重其他国家根据国际法，特别是《联合国海洋法公约》享有的海洋权利。
菲律宾国防部发表此声明的前一天，中国国防部发言人陈曦在被问及菲律宾与澳大利亚近日签署的防务合作协议时，指责菲律宾“个别政客”“妄图拉拢外部势力”“搅局”南中国海。
陈曦还表示，此类举动“只会加剧局势紧张，破坏地区稳定”。
他还呼吁“有关域外国家应切实尊重中方在南海的主权和权益，停止插手介入南海问题。”他同时警告说，北京将继续采取所谓的“必要措施有力应对侵权挑衅行为。”
11月15日，菲律宾国防部长吉尔伯托·特奥多罗(Gilberto Teodoro Jr.)与澳大利亚驻菲律宾大使马克·伊内斯-布朗(Marc Innes-Brown)在马尼拉南港签署了签署了一项称为“菲律宾-澳大利亚防务合作安排”的新的国防协议，旨在加强合作，简化两国联合军事行动的协调程序，“加强嚇阻”中国在南中国海的军事扩张。
特奥多罗当时指出，该协议将为双方在海、空、陆军力量，以及人道主义援助和救灾方面的更紧密合作铺平道路，并将增强菲律宾的“可信威慑态势”，包括在南中国海地区。澳大利亚总理安东尼·阿尔巴尼斯(Anthony Albanese)在马尼拉见证了这项防务协议的签署。
两国还对南中国海海域针对菲律宾公民和菲律宾船只的挑衅和危险行为表示关切，并重申了2016年南中国海仲裁裁决的约束力。该裁决否定了中国在南中国海提出的历史性权利主张的法律依据。北京拒绝接受该裁决。
不仅是澳大利亚和菲律宾支持2016年国际仲裁裁决的约束力，今年7月11日，菲、澳以及美国等14个国家就南中国海仲裁案裁决10周年发表联合声明，再次确认这项裁决具有法律约束力。14国重申了仲裁庭的裁决，宣布中国在南中国海的扩张性海事主张没有法律依据。
美国、菲律宾、日本、澳大利亚和英国等14国就南中国海仲裁案裁决10周年发表联合声明

# 台湾九合一地方选举：台当局警告选举面临北京干预风险

台湾九合一地方选举周五（11月27日）进入竞选活动最后一天，选民将于周六投票。北京密切关注此次选举。台湾国防部通报称，侦测到中国军机活动再度激增。台湾当局此前警告，选举面临北京干预的风险。

法新社报道，这场四年一度的选举将在全台22个县市选出近1.1万名地方公职人员，包括县市长。投票将于当地时间周六上午8时（格林尼治时间零时）开始，下午4时结束，结果预计当晚揭晓。

主张与中国大陆加强关系的国民党是台湾历史最悠久的政党，此次力争保住2022年赢得的14个县市长席位。台湾总统赖清德所属的民进党则希望在现有5席的基础上再有斩获。

投票日前，两大政党的候选人都避谈来自中国大陆的威胁，将竞选重点放在民众购买力问题上。不过，负责大陆政策的台湾大陆委员会表示，北京已采取多种手段试图影响选举结果，包括陆委会所称的“认知战”和“跨国镇压”。

台北市长选战胶着 支持者自制丝带拉票

在国民党执政近30年的台北，现任市长蒋万安迎战民进党籍立法委员沈伯洋。蒋万安被视为未来可能角逐总统职位的人选。

沈伯洋参选之初并不被看好，但如今已追上立场亲北京的对手，竞选集会吸引了大批民众。沈伯洋对北京持强烈批评立场，中国大陆警方正以涉嫌从事“分裂活动”为由追查他。

台北一些市民自制并分发丝带，为自己支持的候选人拉票。这些丝带宽几厘米、长逾半米，在沈伯洋的支持者中尤其流行。有人用来装饰店铺，也有人把丝带系在头发、包袋或宠物身上。

台湾人口最多的城市新北市是国民党的另一处票仓，市长选举同样受到密切关注。

分析人士指出，地方选举结果难以用来预测选民在2028年总统选举中的投票取向，但周六的结果可能影响各党如何提名总统候选人。

Blog War Chinese v American Views on WAR with Taiwan
Chinese v American Views on WAR with Taiwan
Posted Aug 14, 2026 by Martin Armstrong |
The Center for Strategic and International Studies conducted an extraordinary survey of 64 leading experts on China, Taiwan, and cross-Strait relations, including 28 former senior U.S. government officials, 23 former government policy and intelligence analysts, and 13 academics and think-tank experts. What their answers reveal is not that China is preparing to invade Taiwan tomorrow, as the neocons would like everyone to believe, but that Beijing remains willing to wait so long as nobody crosses the line of formal Taiwanese independence. Some 84% said Beijing is willing to wait for unification but will not accept the status quo permanently, while only 10% believed China seeks unification at the earliest opportunity. Not one of the 64 experts believed Beijing would ever accept an independent Taiwan.
This is precisely why Taiwan has become so dangerous. The West keeps portraying the conflict as if Xi Jinping wakes up every morning staring at a calendar trying to decide when to launch an amphibious invasion. Yet 83% of these experts said China did not plan to use significant kinetic force against Taiwan by 2027, and 80% said China’s enormous 2022 military exercises did not indicate Beijing had accelerated its timetable. Only 6% of respondents outside the former senior government group saw 2027 as a hard deadline, while not one former senior U.S. official did. The obsession with 2027 has nevertheless become extremely useful for the military establishment because every supposed deadline becomes another justification for weapons, deployments, bases, and spending.
The survey found that 44% believed Beijing has a hard deadline of 2049, the centennial of the People’s Republic, while 42% believed China could wait indefinitely provided unification remains possible. This is an important distinction because China thinks in terms of generations while Western politicians think in terms of the next election. Beijing does not need to invade Taiwan if economic, political, and military pressure can gradually change the situation in its favor. Only 20% of those surveyed believed China even possessed a coherent roadmap for peaceful unification, which tells us this is not some perfectly scripted invasion plan sitting in Xi’s desk drawer.
Where the numbers become alarming is not an unprovoked invasion but what happens when politicians begin crossing China’s red lines. More than three-quarters of the experts, 77%, believed China would invade within six months if Taiwan formally declared independence. Among former senior U.S. officials, that number was 79%. Even some of those who did not expect an immediate invasion believed Beijing would respond with a blockade or enormous military exercises. This is why politicians encouraging Taiwan toward formal independence are playing with the lives of 23 million people. They can deliver all the speeches they want about democracy from Washington, London, or Brussels, but they will not be the civilians sitting underneath the missiles if their political experiment goes wrong.
Not one expert believed an explicit American commitment to defend Taiwan would cause China to invade immediately, but 64% believed Beijing would respond strongly enough to provoke a U.S.-China or China-Taiwan crisis, while another 31% expected a more limited negative response. Only two of the 64 experts believed formally committing America to Taiwan’s defense would actually deter China from using force because Beijing already assumes that the United States will intervene anyway.
A direct invasion is not even the most likely path toward conflict. Only 8% of the experts described an amphibious invasion within ten years as likely, while 63% called it possible and 27% unlikely. Force short of invasion received much higher probabilities, with 52% saying deliberate escalation such as a blockade was likely or very likely. An accidental military incident was considered even more dangerous, with 34% saying a collision or accident around the Taiwan Strait was likely and another 22% calling it very likely. When warships and aircraft from opposing nuclear powers continually operate around the same small body of water, war does not require some grand master plan. It requires one mistake followed by politicians who refuse to back down.
A later CSIS survey of American and Taiwanese experts reinforces that point. Roughly 90% of U.S. experts and 62% of Taiwanese experts believed China already possessed the capability to impose a law-enforcement-led quarantine that substantially reduces trade into Taiwan. Around 80% of American experts and 60% of Taiwanese experts believed Beijing could execute a PLA blockade, while Taiwanese experts were considerably more skeptical that China could successfully carry out an invasion. If Beijing wanted to coerce Taiwan during the following five years, experts considered a quarantine the most likely option. If China decided it wanted immediate unification, however, approximately 80% regarded a highly kinetic joint blockade as likely or very likely.
This is where the economic consequences become enormous because Taiwan does not need to be invaded for the world economy to be thrown into chaos. A quarantine or blockade would immediately threaten shipping, insurance, semiconductor supply chains, electronics, automobiles, communications equipment, and virtually every modern industry dependent upon advanced chips. The later CSIS survey found most American and Taiwanese experts did not believe Taiwan could withstand a Chinese blockade for longer than three months without substantial U.S. intervention. Washington would then face the decision nobody wants to discuss honestly: accept China’s blockade or attempt to break it militarily and risk direct war between two nuclear powers.
Taiwan is also the world’s semiconductor pressure point. The island’s importance to advanced chip manufacturing means a serious blockade would not remain a regional event. Factories thousands of miles away could discover that a conflict they thought had nothing to do with them suddenly prevents them from obtaining critical components. Markets would begin repricing the risk immediately, shipping premiums would explode, companies would scramble for inventory, and governments would discover once again how fragile global supply chains have become. This is why capital will react long before politicians formally declare that a war has begun.
What I find particularly revealing in the later CSIS survey is the difference between American confidence and Taiwanese confidence in Washington. An astonishing 96% of American experts were completely or moderately confident that the United States would intervene militarily if China invaded Taiwan during the following five years. Taiwanese experts were less confident in American intervention and considerably less confident that U.S. allies would join the fight. It is always easier for people thousands of miles away to be certain about somebody else’s war.
This is precisely why Taiwan remains one of the critical geopolitical pressure points as we move toward 2029. The danger is not simply that China arbitrarily decides to invade. The greater danger is escalation, miscalculation, political promises that cannot be withdrawn, and Western policymakers convincing themselves that every additional provocation somehow produces deterrence. China has made its position on formal independence perfectly clear, and even the experts inside the Western foreign-policy establishment overwhelmingly acknowledge that Beijing would react with force if that line were crossed.
If Taiwan declares formal independence, 77% of the experts surveyed believed China would invade within six months. That is not a statistic policymakers should treat as another war-game scenario. It is a warning about what happens when politicians deliberately remove the ambiguity that has helped keep the peace.
