content:
Fundraiser by Hunter Ross : HELP NEPAL & TIBET FLOOD VICTIMS RECOVER AND REBUILD
This fund brings emergency supplies, shelter, and rebuilding to Nepal and Tibet communities
Inspire others and help Hunter build momentum.
Inspire others and help Hunter build momentum.
Hunter Ross is organizing this fundraiser.
Help Nepal Recover From Devastating Floods
My name is Hunter Ross, and I am from Dallas, Texas, USA. I am organizing this fundraiser to help provide relief to people and communities affected by devastating flooding in Nepal and Tibet.
Nepal has become much more than a country I visit. Over the years, I have developed a deep personal connection to Nepal through frequent travel, volunteering, environmental work, tourism development, and relationships with local communities.
I travel to Nepal approximately three times a year and have actively volunteered in efforts related to environmental conservation, sustainable tourism, and local community development. Through these experiences, I have met many wonderful people and developed relationships with individuals and communities who have welcomed me and shared their lives and culture with me.
I am not raising these funds because I am a government agency or large relief organization. I am an individual from Dallas who has spent years visiting Nepal, volunteering there, and building personal connections with people in the country. I want to use those connections and my experience in Nepal to help support people whose lives and livelihoods have been affected by flooding.
Severe flooding can have devastating consequences for communities in Nepal and Tibet.
Heavy rainfall, rising rivers, and flooding can damage or destroy homes, roads, bridges, farmland, businesses, and other essential infrastructure. Families can lose their possessions, crops, livestock, and sources of income.
In rural and mountainous areas, the consequences can be even more serious. When roads and bridges are damaged or washed away, entire communities can become isolated and difficult to reach. Access to food, clean drinking water, medical care, transportation, and other essential services can be severely disrupted.
Flooding can also create serious sanitation and health risks when drinking-water systems are contaminated or damaged.
The need does not end when the water recedes. Families and communities may require assistance for weeks or months as they clean their homes, replace essential belongings, repair buildings, restore access to roads and water systems, and rebuild their livelihoods.
My Relationship to the People I Am Raising Funds For
My relationship with the people I am trying to help comes from my years of travel, volunteering, environmental work, tourism development, and personal relationships in Nepal.
Because I regularly travel to Nepal and have spent significant time working with and learning from local communities, I have developed a strong connection to the people and places affected by these disasters.
I want to use this fundraiser to provide assistance to people who are directly affected by flooding, particularly vulnerable families and communities that may have difficulty accessing assistance.
I will be transparent with donors about where the money goes and will provide updates as the relief effort progresses.
How the $50,000 Will Be Spent
Our fundraising goal is $50,000.
The funds will be used for flood-relief and recovery needs. Depending on the circumstances and the most urgent needs identified on the ground, donations may be used for:
Emergency food and drinking water for affected families
Medical supplies and basic healthcare needs
Temporary shelter and essential household necessities
Clothing, blankets, and other emergency supplies
Assistance for families whose homes have been damaged or destroyed
Support for farmers and families who have lost crops, livestock, equipment, or other sources of livelihood
Transportation and delivery of relief supplies to affected communities
Repair or restoration of essential community resources and infrastructure where appropriate
Assistance to vulnerable families and remote communities that may be difficult to reach through traditional relief efforts
The exact allocation will depend on the needs identified in the affected communities at the time the funds are distributed.
I understand that I am accountable for using the money raised in the manner described in this campaign. I will make every effort to ensure that donations are used responsibly, transparently, and for legitimate flood-relief and recovery purposes.
Transparency is extremely important to me.
I want every person who contributes to understand who I am, why I am doing this, who the fundraiser is intended to help, and how the money will be used.
As the campaign progresses, I will provide updates regarding fundraising, relief efforts, and the use of donations whenever possible.
If circumstances change and a particular relief need is no longer present, funds may be directed toward another legitimate and urgent flood-recovery need within the affected communities rather than being left unused.
Nepal has given me incredible experiences, friendships, and memories. I have been fortunate to return to the country many times, and I have seen firsthand the generosity and resilience of the people there.
Now, I want to give something back.
A donation of $10, $50, $100, $500, or any amount you can afford can contribute to helping a family recover from a devastating event.
If you cannot donate, sharing this fundraiser with your friends, family, coworkers, and social networks can be just as valuable. Reaching more people gives us a greater chance of reaching our $50,000 goal.
Fundraising Goal: $50,000
This campaign is about more than raising money. It is about standing with people who have lost homes, belongings, livelihoods, and a sense of security because of flooding.
I have spent years visiting and volunteering in Nepal, and I believe this is an opportunity to give back to communities that have given me so much.
Please consider donating and sharing this fundraiser.
Together, we can help provide immediate necessities while supporting the long process of recovery and rebuilding.
Thank you for taking the time to read my story, for caring about the people affected by these floods, and for supporting this effort.
Your donation starts Hunter’s journey to success by inspiring others to help.

台湾2026年GDP增速预测上调至13.28%，为1978年以来最高
台湾2026年GDP增长预测上调至13.28%，为1978年以来最高
要激活文字转语音服务，请首先同意以下隐私政策。
中新社台北11月27日电 台湾主计总署(DGBAS)周五表示，全球对人工智能(AI)应用的强劲需求预计将维持第四季度经济强劲增长，预计2026年台湾经济将增长13.28%，创48年来最快增速。
DGBAS 将台湾 2026 年国内生产总值 (GDP) 增长预测上调至 13.28%，比 8 月份的预测提高了 2.23 个百分点。如果实现的话，增长率将是1978年以来的最高水平，当时该国经济增长了13.56%。
国家统计局初步数据显示，第三季度台湾GDP增长14.39%，较之前预测的14.36%上升0.03个百分点。
DGBAS表示，第四季度GDP增速预计将达到10.42%，比之前的预测上调5.05个百分点。
DGBAS表示，台湾的高科技出口预计将继续受益于全球对人工智能应用快速增长的需求，而非科技行业出口的复苏预计将提供额外的支持。
统计局表示，预计2026年台湾货物和服务出口将同比增长23.96%，较之前预测上调2.68个百分点；进口预计将增长21.41%，上调0.26个百分点。
根据 DGBAS 的数据，台湾的商品出口预计将从 2025 年的约 6400 亿美元增至 2026 年的创纪录的 9386.4 亿美元，并在 2027 年超过 1.11 万亿美元。
在全球人工智能基础设施强劲需求的推动下，预计2026年台湾民间投资将增长14.90%，较之前预测上升3.32个百分点。 DGBAS 表示，固定资本形成预计将增长 12.77%。
DGBAS 表示，随着企业盈利的改善，企业似乎越来越愿意支付奖金和提高工资。
这些因素，加上汽车市场的复苏和旅游业的持续增长，预计将支持私人消费，预计 2026 年私人消费将增长 4.74%。
然而，消费增长预测较之前的预测下调了 0.02 个百分点，反映了 DGBAS 对近期该国股市波动的评估。
展望2027年，DGBAS预计台湾经济将增长6.51%，比之前的预测上升0.47个百分点。
由于全球市场原油、消费电子产品和国内食品价格上涨，预计 2026 年消费者价格指数 (CPI) 将上涨 2.07%，超过央行衡量通胀压力的 2% 门槛。
DGBAS表示，预计2027年通胀压力将有所缓解，CPI增速预计将放缓至1.96%。
2027年人均GDP将超过5万美元
人工智能繁荣给台湾带来了巨大的经济利益，预计人均GDP将从2025年的39,580美元增至2026年的46,767美元。
预计2027年台湾人均GDP将进一步上升至50,779美元，在全球主要经济体中排名第29位。

Taiwan's 2026 GDP growth forecast raised to 13.28%, highest since 1978 - Focus Taiwan
Taiwan's 2026 GDP growth forecast raised to 13.28%, highest since 1978
To activate the text-to-speech service, please first agree to the privacy policy below.
Taipei, Nov. 27 (CNA) Taiwan's economy is forecast to grow 13.28 percent in 2026, the fastest pace in 48 years, as robust global demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications is expected to sustain strong economic growth through the fourth quarter, the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) said Friday.
The DGBAS raised its forecast for Taiwan's 2026 gross domestic product (GDP) growth to 13.28 percent, up 2.23 percentage points from its previous estimate in August. If realized, the growth rate would be the highest since 1978, when the country's economy grew 13.56 percent.
In a preliminary reading, the DGBAS said Taiwan's GDP grew 14.39 percent in the third quarter, up 0.03 percentage points from its previous estimate of 14.36 percent.
Fourth-quarter GDP growth is projected to reach 10.42 percent, an upward revision of 5.05 percentage points from the previous forecast, the DGBAS said.
The DGBAS said Taiwan's high-tech exports are expected to continue benefiting from rapidly growing global demand for AI applications, while a recovery in exports from non-tech industries is expected to provide additional support.
Taiwan's exports of goods and services are forecast to grow 23.96 percent year on year in 2026, up 2.68 percentage points from the previous estimate, while imports are projected to rise 21.41 percent, an upward revision of 0.26 percentage points, the DGBAS said.
Taiwan's merchandise exports are expected to reach a record US$938.64 billion in 2026, up from about US$640 billion in 2025, and exceed US$1.11 trillion in 2027, according to the DGBAS.
Driven by strong global demand for AI infrastructure, private investment in Taiwan is forecast to grow 14.90 percent in 2026, up 3.32 percentage points from the previous estimate. Fixed capital formation is projected to increase 12.77 percent, the DGBAS said.
As corporate earnings improve, companies appear increasingly willing to pay bonuses and raise wages, the DGBAS said.
These factors, along with a recovery in the auto market and continued growth in tourism, are expected to support private consumption, which is forecast to grow 4.74 percent in 2026.
The consumption growth forecast, however, was revised downward by 0.02 percentage points from the previous estimate, reflecting the DGBAS' assessment of recent volatility in the country's stock market.
Looking ahead to 2027, the DGBAS expects Taiwan's economy to grow 6.51 percent, up 0.47 percentage points from its previous forecast.
The consumer price index (CPI) is projected to rise 2.07 percent in 2026, exceeding the 2 percent threshold the central bank uses to gauge inflationary pressures, amid rising prices for crude oil on global markets, consumer electronics and domestic food products.
Inflationary pressures are expected to ease in 2027, with CPI growth forecast to slow to 1.96 percent, the DGBAS said.
GDP per capita to exceed US$50,000 in 2027
The AI boom has brought substantial economic benefits to Taiwan, with GDP per capita expected to reach US$46,767 in 2026, up from US$39,580 in 2025, the DGBAS said.
The figure is expected to rise further in 2027 to US$50,779, ranking Taiwan No. 29 among the world's major economies in GDP per capita, the DGBAS said.
Despite the AI boom, Tsai Yu-tai (蔡鈺泰), head of the DGBAS Department of Statistics, said potential downside risks include further U.S. restrictions on semiconductor exports to China and potential tighter regulation of AI development.
The DGBAS has therefore adopted a slightly cautious approach in projecting Taiwan's export growth, Tsai said, emphasizing that global supply of AI-related products continues to fall short of demand.

content:
Fundraiser by Uyghur Anthology : Support the Contemporary Uyghur Anthology
This anthology funds Uyghur writers and artists, translation, events, and community growth
Uyghur Anthology is organizing this fundraiser.
The Contemporary Uyghur Anthology is a publication that platforms Uyghur (and anyone drawing their roots from East Turkistan) artists and writers in the diaspora by providing a space that is often inaccessible to those in our community. There are no other projects of its kind in the English language, and with two volumes already published, we hope to take this project to the next level. It's a rare look at Uyghur expression in an environment where all our stories are told by people pushing their own narratives without the intimate knowledge of our lived experiences.
<"Manifesto" by Sumayah Jurad from Vol. II>
We asked ourselves these questions - why wait for others to invite us to the table when we can pull up a chair and introduce ourselves? Why let others speak for us without trying first to speak? Our broken English can only be improved with audacity, and world literature is only enriched by the presence of new voices.
All-in-all, our efforts have been met with support from our community and pleasant surprise from those who did not know what they did not know.
Somewhat unprecedented is that we publish the authors' original language alongside the translation. Our book is filled with Uyghur, Latin, Cyrillic, and Chinese script to encapsulate as much of our community's experience as we can.
There are many publications in diaspora communities that platform East and South Asians, SEA, MENA, and more. Central Asia is often underrepresented in world literature or Asia-specific publications, and occupied territories even less so. Uyghurs themselves have been a relatively new diaspora community in English-speaking countries, and haven't had the opportunities to grow their literary or artistic communities. Many don't have the tools to nurture their talents, or knowledge of creative networks or opportunities, even when many journals seek work from underrepresented groups. In instances where they are aware, it's difficult to be published in this competitive field without the education and styles that publications look for. There are only a handful of literary translators translating from Uyghur to English, and not many Uyghurs who have had the chances to develop their creative language when learning English.
To sum up, the issues were:
No spaces for Uyghur writers and artists to develop their skills
A disconnect from artist communities, be it local or online
No bridge between our native tongue and English, and in turn, world literature
So, we put together a small group at the Tarim Network to take on this challenge. Completely volunteer-run; the very essence of a passion project. We did a call-out for anything and all. New writers, established writers, any language, any genre, whatever we could print in a book. And here we were, the first book of its kind, created to speak for ourselves without outsider voices, without a publishing house, raw and straight from the source.
<From the launch of Vol. I at Harvard University>
"The Contemporary Uyghur Anthology is a collection of Uyghur reflections in diaspora. Weaving together memories of the homeland, experiences of displacement, and transitions of identities, this anthology is a creative reflection of the beauty and complexities of the Uyghur experience.
By centering Uyghur voices at the forefront, this anthology serves as a form of living memory in a pivotal moment of Uyghur history. The title Under the Mulberry Tree refers to a story from the Uyghur literary classic Ana Yurt, where youthful Nuri faces terrible injustices, separation, and turmoil; but for one moment in the Charbagh, his love for Sebihe and his own family is full, ripe, and sweet, like the mulberries from the ancient tree. In a similar way that the mulberry tree offered comforts in Nuri’s time of need, we hope this volume offers a place of reflection and celebration of Uyghur culture."
We'd partnered with a member from a Jewish organisation to run writing workshops and explain editorial processes, as we had never worked on something like this before. After that collaboration, we decided to publish a revised edition on our own. This time, we added editors' notes to the pages to explain certain terms and historical and cultural contexts - mainly for our own youth, who don't always have access to cultural education. We translated more pieces from Uyghur and Chinese. Our contributors spanned 13 countries, at all levels of experience.
Was this work sustainable? Equipped with the tools, experience, and outpouring of support from our first volume, we spent the next two years saying yes. Our first book was now in libraries, there were articles and academic papers that mentioned it, and most of all, we reaffirmed the need for this sort of work. Not only were we accepting submissions, we worked one-on-one with emerging writers and artists to edit their pieces. We also helped first-time translators have their first publications with help from more experienced translators, as well as connecting them with the original authors.
Our second volume was even better than the last. From the blurb:
"How do we respond to the unexpected, and how does it influence perceptions of ourselves or the environments in which we exist? As a diaspora population, unexpected encounters can shape and transform what it means to be Uyghur as we build a new life outside of the homeland. Encounters Under the Mulberry Tree takes on the literal, abstract, and expanded renditions of these moments. We feature contemporary and historical works, including art, poetry, and prose in five languages with contributors based in a dozen countries, from established writers like award-winning author and filmmaker Tahir Hamut Izgil, to emerging artists, writers and translators of all ages. This book is a library of vignettes that grapple with intersections and how we make sense of it all."
Five languages (Uyghur, English, Chinese, Russian, Turkish)
<Vol. II showcased at a college hosted by Rawan Mentorship>
Now we embark on our third volume. The three of us do this while maintaining full time jobs, academic careers, and other side projects. We all live in different countries and have only met in person once. But it's something that we need to do, for our community and for ourselves. Our contributors have gained so much from this experience and we want to extend this opportunity to more people. This needs to survive in order for similar initiatives to be born.
Supporting the editors - all expenses so far have been paid out-of-pocket or through book sales. We do not have any donors or sponsors (yet!).
Supporting our contributors - we cannot afford to pay any of our contributors. Despite this, we have given free copies of the book to contributors, but this is definitely leaving a dent in our pockets.
Recruiting more people - paid internships or remuneration for one-off work would help volunteers spend more time on this project in this economy.
Enhance our level of expertise - we want to improve. Workshops or courses for our editors and contributors, professional feedback, the works. Unfortunately there is no one who speaks Uyghur and who is involved in Western publishing or English literature on a professional or academic level. We would appreciate connections with professionals from any language background, or the funding to level up.
Expand our network - we'd love to promote our work at literary festivals, go to conferences, do book events, establish ourselves in the public eye, provide reader copies to reviewers, and so on. However, there is a funding barrier to overcome to be able to attend these events, organise, or pre-order books.
<Vol. I on display at the Mosquers Film Festival, 2025>
Munawwar Abdulla is an Uyghur advocate, poet, and scientist born on unceded Kaurna land (Australia) and based in Massachusetts. She co-founded The Tarim Network, runs Uyghur Collective, and collaborates on projects with Uyghur rights organisations around the world. Her writings and literary translations have been published in places such as Modern Poetry in Translation, Asymptote, the Margins, the Georgia Review, and others.
Sonya Imin is a mixed Uyghur American scholar and multi-disciplinary creative who has worked on art and film projects across the US, Europe, and Central Asia. Growing up between the borderlands of the Uyghur homeland, broader Central Asia, and the midwestern United States, interrogations of belonging, home, and displacement influence the nature of her work. Currently based in Brussels, she is working on her doctoral research on Uyghur artistic production in the diaspora.
Maidina Kadeer is a mixed Uyghur-Hui writer and editor, born in Ghulja and currently based in Montreal (Tiohtià:ke), Canada. She holds a BA in English Literature and Law and Society from Concordia University, with a focus on post- and neo-colonial literature. Her work explores Uyghur identity, history, and culture through cuisine, agriculture, and neo-colonialism. She has contributed to projects such as a poem, NinetySix, in Slavs and Tatars’ Contest of the Fruits (2021) and participates in panels and interviews on Agriculture and Food History to raise awareness about Uyghur culture.

content:
台湾经济连续11个月“蓬勃发展”创历史新高 - 聚焦台湾
台湾经济连续11个月“蓬勃发展” 创历史新高
要激活文字转语音服务，请首先同意以下隐私政策。
中新社台北11月27日电 国家发展委员会(NDC)周五表示，10月份台湾经济连续第11个月亮起红灯，表明台湾经济正在蓬勃发展，并可能出现过热，这是有记录以来最长的连续亮灯状态。
NDC经济发展处处长陈美菊表示，台湾经济研究所的一项调查显示，电子及资讯科技企业对未来仍持谨慎乐观态度，而石化及运输设备制造商则不太乐观。
不过，陈表示，总体而言，对经济前景持乐观态度的企业多于悲观企业。
陈说，10月份综合得分为40分，比9月份的41分下降1分，但监测指标仍处于红色区域，表明经济强劲增长。
在国家数据中心的五色系统下，红灯表示经济蓬勃发展或可能过热，而黄红色则表示状况有所改善。绿色代表经济状况稳定，黄蓝色代表经济放缓，蓝色代表经济低迷。
在构成该指数的九个组成部分中，制造业景气指标从黄红色变为绿灯，而其他八个指标则保持不变。
陈表示，下降主要归因于制造业商业环境的变化。
她表示，虽然人工智能相关需求继续支撑台湾经济，但包括美国中期选举在内的国际政治和经济发展削弱了一些企业的信心。
展望未来，国家数据中心表示，人工智能的更深入采用以及主要国际云服务提供商（CSP）资本支出的持续增加预计将促进台湾供应链的出口。
该委员会表示，随着当地科技公司扩大产能以满足全球人工智能需求，并增加研发支出以增强竞争力，预计投资也将获得动力。
报告补充称，在消费方面，稳定的就业市场和强劲的企业盈利预计将通过奖金和股息支付来支持家庭支出。
不过，NDC表示，中期选举后美国贸易政策的不确定性、地缘政治的发展以及全球货币政策的走向值得密切关注。
当被问及11月份股市波动时，陈表示，受影响最大的公司主要是面临周期性融资相关资金压力的新兴CSP。
她表示，相比之下，规模较大的通信服务提供商拥有更多元化的收入来源、更多的资源和更强的定价能力，预计收入将继续增长。

Taiwan's economy 'booming' for 11th straight month, setting a record
To activate the text-to-speech service, please first agree to the privacy policy below.
Taipei, Nov. 27 (CNA) Taiwan's economy flashed a red light for the 11th consecutive month in October -- indicating it was booming and potentially overheating -- marking the longest such streak on record, the National Development Council (NDC) said on Friday.
NDC Department of Economic Development Director Chen Mei-chu (陳美菊) said a survey by the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research found that electronics and information technology companies remained cautiously optimistic about the future, while petrochemical and transportation equipment manufacturers were less optimistic.
Overall, however, Chen said more businesses remained optimistic about the economic outlook than pessimistic.
The composite score for October stood at 40 points, down one point from 41 in September, but the monitoring indicator remained in the red zone, signaling strong economic growth, Chen said.
Under the NDC's five-color system, a red light indicates a booming economy or possible overheating, while yellow-red signals improving conditions. Green represents stable economic conditions, yellow-blue indicates a slowdown, and blue signals a sluggish economy.
Of the nine components making up the index, the manufacturing business climate indicator shifted from a yellow-red to a green light, while the other eight indicators remained unchanged.
Chen said the decline was mainly attributable to the change in the manufacturing business climate.
While AI-related demand continued to support Taiwan's economy, international political and economic developments, including the U.S. midterm elections, had dampened confidence among some businesses,she said.
Looking ahead, the NDC said deeper adoption of AI and continued increases in capital spending by major international cloud service providers (CSPs) are expected to boost exports from Taiwan's supply chains.
Investment is also expected to gain momentum as local technology companies expand production capacity to meet global AI demand and increase research and development spending to strengthen their competitiveness, the council said.
On the consumption front, a stable job market and stronger corporate earnings are expected to support household spending through bonuses and dividend payments, it added.
However, the NDC said uncertainties over U.S. trade policies following the midterm elections, geopolitical developments and the direction of global monetary policy warrant close monitoring.
Asked about stock market volatility in November, Chen said the companies most affected were mainly emerging CSPs facing funding pressures related to cyclical financing.
Larger CSPs, by contrast, have more diversified revenue streams, greater resources, and stronger pricing power, and are expected to continue growing their revenue, she said.

Hackers breach U.S. Air Force flagship Cloud One computing platform
The hacking of the U.S. Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform could jeopardize a vast swath of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data. | REUTERS
X Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Bluesky Threads Email Print Bookmark story Copy link
Washington – Hackers have breached the U.S. Air Force’s flagship cloud computing platform, three people familiar with the matter said, in a development that could jeopardize a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.
The intrusion at Cloud One was discovered within the past month or so during work to upgrade the system, two of the people said, adding that the discovery has led to disruption across the platform. Reporters could not establish the identity of the hackers, the full scope of the intrusion or whether any data had been stolen.
In a statement, the Air Force said it “does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the Air Force) information, systems and mission capabilities.”

summary: 中国部署越来越大的无人货运飞机的野心正在不断增强，白鲸航空推出了 W8000 货运无人机，据报道，这款货运无人机设计可承载 8 吨（略低于 18,000 磅）。该飞机代表了该公司自主货运航空计划的重大扩展，恰逢其较小的 W5000 已开始飞行测试。参观者在珠海 W8000 前合影。来自中国互联网 W5000（左）停在珠海的 W8000 旁边。来自中国互联网 W8000先于中国国际航空展亮相珠海
content:
中国部署越来越大的无人货运飞机的野心正在不断增强，白鲸航空推出了 W8000 货运无人机，据报道，这款货运无人机设计可承载 8 吨（略低于 18,000 磅）。该飞机代表了该公司自主货运航空计划的重大扩展，恰逢其较小的 W5000 已开始飞行测试。参观者在珠海 W8000 前合影。来自中国互联网 W5000（左）停在珠海的 W8000 旁边。来自中国互联网 W8000 在中国国际航空航天博览会（俗称中国航展）之前亮相珠海。在 12 月 7 日该活动开幕之前，我们已经抢先了解了一个平台，该平台旨在将无人货运能力提升到目前仅限于传统载人运输机的水平。据报道，其有效载荷为 8 吨，远高于 W5000，后者的设计载荷可达 5 吨（11,000 磅）。与 W5000 一样，W8000 可以通过后坡道装卸。 W8000 尾部的翻盖式门和后装载坡道。然而目前，双涡轮螺旋桨飞机 W8000 仍然是一个开发概念。其有效载荷数字只是设计目标，其航程、最大起飞重量和操作要求等细节仍不清楚。
为了进行比较，八吨的有效载荷将使 W8000 与 DHC-5 Buffalo 双引擎涡轮螺旋桨短距起降运输机处于同一类别。无论如何，此次亮相凸显了白鲸航空开发一系列大型无人驾驶货运飞机的雄心，目标是区域货运、偏远地区物流和潜在的军事运输任务，在这些任务中，自主飞机可以比传统货运业务提供优势。珠海W8000的后视图。来自中国互联网 双涡轮螺旋桨飞机 W8000 动力装置所使用的发动机尚未确定。通过中国互联网 更大的无人运输 W8000 的有效负载能力将使其能够运输大型设备、托盘货物、工业用品和其他大件货物。在商业环境中，大型自主货运飞机在公路或铁路基础设施有限或传统航空运输过于昂贵而无法频繁运营的航线上特别有用。尽管消除了机上机组人员，但飞机仍然需要维护人员、地勤人员、货物装载基础设施和支持性运营网络。最终，该飞机也可能被批准在受控空域内运行，取代载人支线货运业务，但这种用例在未来仍有一段路要走。不可避免的是，该飞机的发展也表明了大型货运无人机的潜在军事意义。
珠海的 W5000 和 W8000。来自中国互联网 W8000 可以为中国人民解放军 (PLA) 提供大量额外的空运选择，以保障在偏远、孤立或基础设施匮乏的地点作战的部队。这在印度-太平洋地区尤其重要，中国不断扩大的军事设施和岛屿前哨网络已经对频繁的补给飞行产生了需求。例如，在南中国海，大型货运无人机可以将设备、医疗用品、备件和其他必需品运输到远程设施，而无需载人运输

【原文 English Original】
China’s ambitions to field increasingly large, uncrewed cargo aircraft are growing, with Air White Whale unveiling its W8000, a cargo UAV reportedly designed to carry up to eight metric tons — a little less than 18,000 pounds. The aircraft represents a significant expansion of the company’s plans for autonomous freight aviation, coming just as its smaller W5000 has begun flight testing. Visitors pose in front of the W8000 at Zhuhai. via Chinese internet The W5000 (left) parked next to the W8000 at Zhuhai. via Chinese internet The W8000 appeared in Zhuhai, ahead of the China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition, commonly known as Airshow China . Before that event opens its doors on December 7, we have gotten an early look at a platform intended to push uncrewed cargo capacity into a class now limited to conventional, crewed transport aircraft. Its reported eight-ton payload would put it substantially above the W5000, which is designed to carry up to five metric tons (11,000 pounds). Like the W5000, the W8000 can be loaded and unloaded via a rear ramp. Clamshell doors and rear loading ramp in the tail of the W8000. via Chinese internet For now, however, the twin-turboprop W8000 remains a developmental concept. Its payload figure is a design target, and details about its range, maximum takeoff weight, and operational requirements are still unclear. For purposes of comparison, an eight-metric-ton payload would put the W8000 in much the same category as the DHC-5 Buffalo twin-engine turboprop STOL transport. Regardless, the unveiling highlights Air White Whale’s ambitions to develop a family of large uncrewed cargo aircraft, targeting regional freight, remote-area logistics, and potentially military transportation missions where autonomous aircraft could offer advantages over conventional cargo operations. Rear view of the W8000 at Zhuhai. via Chinese internet The engines used in the powerplant for the twin-turboprop W8000 are yet to be identified. via Chinese internet An Even Bigger Uncrewed Transport The W8000’s payload capacity would allow it to transport large equipment, palletized freight, industrial supplies, and other bulky cargo. In a commercial context, large autonomous cargo aircraft could be particularly useful on routes where road or rail infrastructure is limited, or where conventional air transport is too expensive to operate frequently. Although eliminating onboard flight crews, the aircraft would still require maintenance personnel, ground handling, cargo-loading infrastructure, and a supporting operational network. Ultimately, the aircraft could also be cleared to operate inside controlled airspace, displacing crewed feeder cargo operations, but that use case is still some way off in the future. Inevitably, the aircraft’s development also points toward the potential military relevance of large cargo UAVs. The W5000 and W8000 at Zhuhai. via Chinese internet The W8000 could offer the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) a substantial additional airlift option for sustaining forces operating from remote, isolated, or infrastructure-poor locations. This is particularly relevant in the Indo-Pacific, where China’s expanding network of military facilities and island outposts is already creating demand for frequent resupply flights. In the South China Sea, for example, large cargo UAVs could potentially transport equipment, medical supplies, spare parts, and other necessities to remote installations without requiring a crewed transport aircraft for every mission. They could also support operations in western China , including remote and high-altitude regions where road infrastructure is limited and conventional air transport can face additional challenges. There are also potential applications in a conflict, where conventional logistics infrastructure could be damaged or otherwise unavailable. Uncrewed transports would remove the risk to aircrews during routine resupply missions through contested airspace, although the aircraft themselves would remain vulnerable. They would also remove the need for combat search and rescue (CSAR) capabilities, which might be impossible to provide in at least some scenarios. Their usefulness would also depend, at least in some cases, on reliable communications, autonomous navigation, and the ability to operate without continuous access to satellite navigation. Profile view of the W8000 at Zhuhai. via Chinese internet W5000 Has Already Begun Flight Testing The W8000’s unveiling comes as Air White Whale’s smaller W5000 has reached a significant development milestone, completing its maiden flight on November 14. The five-ton cargo UAV reportedly conducted a roughly 30-minute test flight after taking off within approximately 600 meters (1,969 feet). During the flight, it reportedly conducted maneuvers and tested autonomous flight functions, datalink communications, propulsion, and flight-control systems before landing. China’s W5000 large cargo UAV has completed its maiden flight in the Ordos region of Inner Mongolia on 14 November. The aircraft reportedly took off after a 600 m (1,969 ft) ground run, climbed to 2,000 m (6,562 ft) and completed a 30-minute test flight. The trial included… pic.twitter.com/NNLqPKbLLZ — Drone Wars (@Drone_Wars_) November 14, 2026 The W5000 is designed to carry up to five metric tons of cargo, with a reported maximum range of 2,600 kilometers (1,616 miles), maximum takeoff weight of 10.8 tons (21,600 pounds), and cargo compartment volume exceeding 65 cubic meters (2,295 cubic feet). The aircraft is powered by twin turboprop engines. Chinese sources claim that Air White Whale has received 835 orders or prospective commitments from domestic logistics companies for the W5000, although the nature of those commitments and how many represent firm purchase contracts remain unclear. Commercial operations are currently planned to begin by the end of 2027, subject to further testing and certification. The W5000’s flight provides an indication of the company’s progress toward developing large uncrewed cargo aircraft, but the W8000 is a considerably more ambitious undertaking. Several other companies are also pursuing increasingly ambitious uncrewed transport aircraft. These include Tengden’s four-engine TB-001D Scorpion D , which first flew in October 2022 and is designed to carry up to 1.5 metric tons (3,307 pounds) of cargo, as well as the Star UAV System-developed AT200, another 1.5-ton-class cargo drone. The TB0D Scorpion D built by China’s Tengden Technology company completed its maiden flight in Sichuan on October 25, 2022. Twitter video screenshot Other designs include the state-owned Aviation Industry Corporation of China’s HH-100 , with a reported payload capacity of around 700 kilograms (1,543 pounds), and the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation’s CH-YH1000 , designed to carry approximately one metric ton (2,205 pounds). While these aircraft vary considerably in size, configuration, and intended missions, their development highlights China’s broader push to establish uncrewed cargo aviation as a viable logistics capability. A demonstrator of China’s HH-100 commercial cargo drone. Photo by Yue Shuhua/VCG via Getty Images VCG Outside of China, there is some other notable activity in this sector. The United States is also pursuing large uncrewed cargo aircraft for military logistics. As we reported , Textron Aviation and autonomy specialist Merlin recently unveiled the Cessna SkyCourier UX, a concept based on the twin-engine Cessna 408 SkyCourier. The proposed aircraft would use Merlin’s autonomous flight system and could carry approximately 6,000 pounds of cargo. Its designers are exploring a cockpit-less configuration with a hydraulically opening nose section for direct cargo loading, as well as kneeling landing gear and integrated loading systems to simplify operations at austere locations. With a reported range of around 900 nautical miles, the SkyCourier UX is intended to support distributed military forces, including across the Pacific, where it could move supplies between larger logistics hubs and smaller, remote operating locations. The U.S. Air Force has also experimented with autonomous Cessna Caravan aircraft through Joby Aviation and its former Xwing autonomy team, including logistics demonstrations across the Pacific. Better known for land vehicles, Oshkosh Defense also recently announced a partnership with Silicon Valley startup Grid Aero, with the aim of building large military cargo drones. These would draw upon Grid Aero’s experience developing the Lifter family, an autonomous aircraft series with modular payload capacity that the company describes as a “pickup truck of the skies.” The Lifter is planned to carry somewhere between 1,000 and 8,000 pounds over a distance of approximately 1,500 miles.  The Grid Aero Lifter. Oshkosh/Grid Aero While the United States is moving slower than China in this space, there is arguably an even stronger operational case for such capabilities in the U.S. military, given the expeditionary nature of a potential conflict across the vast distances of the Indo-Pacific . Sustaining forces spread across widely separated islands, remote airfields, and austere forward operating locations would place enormous demands on conventional airlift and sealift networks. China Targets A New Class Of Cargo Aviation Overall, the development of the W5000 and W8000 highlights China’s growing interest in cargo UAVs capable of moving freight measured in metric tons rather than kilograms. While smaller delivery drones are increasingly being explored for last-mile transportation, aircraft such as the W8000 are aimed at moving substantial loads between logistics hubs without requiring an onboard crew. If the W8000 progresses, it could eventually offer a heavier transport option alongside the W5000, allowing Air White Whale to target different cargo requirements and routes. The W5000 and W8000 at Zhuhai ahead of Airshow China. via Chinese internet For now, the W8000 points to where Air White Whale wants to take its cargo UAV program. The W5000’s flight-test program will be an important step in establishing whether the company can turn its designs into operational aircraft and start to offer a new class of uncrewed airlift. title: China’s Naval Developments Set For The Spotlight At Zhuhai Airshow
zh_title: 中国海军发展成为珠海航展的焦点
summary: 中国人民解放军海军表示，正在准备在即将于珠海举行的第十六届中国国际航空航天博览会上进行重要亮相，军舰、舰载机、先进武器系统和无人平台将成为重点展示。扩大后的海军部分将包括在海湾另一边的高栏港设立一个新的海事装备展区，这标志着解放军海军首次在此次活动中设立这样的专门展示区。珠海已成为国际防务、航空领域最重要的赛事之一
content:
中国人民解放军海军表示，正在准备在即将于珠海举行的第十六届中国国际航空航天博览会上进行重要亮相，军舰、舰载机、先进武器系统和无人平台将成为重点展示。扩大后的海军部分将包括在海湾另一边的高栏港设立一个新的海事装备展区，这标志着解放军海军首次在此次活动中设立这样的专门展示区。珠海已成为国际国防和航空航天史上最重要的活动之一，成为中国快速发展的航空和军事工业的主要公开展示地。两年一度的中国国际航空航天展览会（俗称中国航展）于 1996 年首次举办，为展示中国一些最先进的军事硬件提供了难得的机会，其中包括在其他地方很少如此详细展示的飞机和系统。虽然该活动也是中国航空航天工业向潜在国际客户推广其产品的主要平台，但它日益成为展示新军事能力和提供难以评估的项目的重要场所。
第十五届中国国际航空航天展览会（又称 2024 年中国航展）于 2024 年 11 月 15 日在中国广东省珠海市中国国际航空航天展览中心举行。摄影：VCG/VCG via Getty Images 前几届已经取得了一些特别重大的进展。 2016 年的展会上，J-20 隐形战斗机首次公开飞行亮相，而 2018 年的展会则以不同寻常的方式展示了这架飞机，包括展示其装载空对空导弹的内部武器舱。 2022年的展会上，歼20首次在珠海进行静态展示，同时还有运20重型运输机、直20直升机以及在展会上进行首次飞行演示的运20空中加油机。最近，2024 年的展会特别引人注目的是 J-35A 隐形战斗机的公开亮相和具有弹射能力的 J-15T 舰​​载战斗机的出现。一架 J-15T 舰​​载战斗机在 2024 年中国航展上进行飞行表演。CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images 今年的展览定于 12 月 7 日至 13 日举行，除其他外，将展示中国海军的广泛能力，特别强调其舰载航空能力的快速发展，这一点我们过去已经详细讨论过。
预计将亮相的最引人注目的飞机包括 J-15T 舰载战斗机、作战型 J-35 隐形战斗机、KJ-600 舰载机载预警和控制 (AEW&C) 飞机、Z-20 直升机的几种海军型号，也许最重要的是新型 JL-15 舰载教练机，它是陆基 JL-10 的发展型。JL-15 舰载教练机的照片突出显示了制动钩和弹射器发射杆。虽然我们之前在珠海见过 J-15T，但如果它配备国产 WS-10H2 发动机，将会引起特别的兴趣。这样的配置将让人们更仔细地了解中国舰载侧卫衍生舰的最新演变

【原文 English Original】
China’s People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) says it’s preparing a major presence at the upcoming 16th China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition in Zhuhai, with warships , carrier-based aircraft , advanced weapons systems, and uncrewed platforms set to feature prominently. The expanded naval component will include a new maritime equipment exhibition area at Gaolan Port, located just on the other side of the bay, marking the first time the PLAN has established such a dedicated display at the event. Zhuhai has become one of the most important events on the international defence and aerospace calendar, serving as China’s principal public showcase for its rapidly developing aviation and military industries. First held in 1996, the biennial China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition, commonly known as Airshow China, provides an unusual opportunity to see some of the country’s most advanced military hardware, including aircraft and systems that are rarely shown in such detail elsewhere. While the event also serves as a major platform for China’s aerospace industry to promote its products to potential international customers , it has increasingly become an important venue for revealing new military capabilities and offering glimpses of programs that are otherwise difficult to assess. A general view of the 15th China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition, or Airshow China 2024, at the China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition Center on November 15, 2024, in Zhuhai, Guangdong Province of China. Photo by VCG/VCG via Getty Images Previous editions have produced some particularly significant developments. The 2016 show saw the J-20 stealth fighter make its first public flying appearance , while the 2018 edition provided an unusually revealing look at the aircraft, including a demonstration of its internal weapons bays, loaded with air-to-air missiles . The 2022 exhibition featured the J-20 on static display for the first time at Zhuhai, alongside the Y-20 heavy transport aircraft, Z-20 helicopter, and YY-20 aerial refueling tanker, which made its first flying demonstration at the event. More recently, the 2024 exhibition was particularly notable for the public debut of the J-35A stealth fighter and the appearance of the catapult-capable J-15T carrier-based fighter. A J-15T carrier-based fighter conducts a flight demonstration at Airshow China 2024. CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images This year’s exhibition, scheduled to take place from December 7 to 13, will showcase, among others, a broad range of the PLAN’s capabilities, with a particularly notable emphasis on the rapid evolution of its carrier aviation capabilities, something we have addressed in detail in the past . Among the most noteworthy aircraft expected to feature are the J-15T carrier-based fighter, the operational J-35 stealth fighter, the KJ-600 carrier-based airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft, several naval variants of the Z-20 helicopter, and, perhaps most significantly, the new JL-15 carrier-capable trainer, a development of the land-based JL-10 . A photo of the JL-15 carrier-capable trainer with the arrestor hook and catapult launch bar highlighted. Chinese internet via X While we have seen the J-15T at Zhuhai before, the aircraft will be of particular interest if it is shown with the indigenous WS-10H2 engine. Such a configuration would offer a closer look at the latest evolution of China’s carrier-based Flanker derivative and its ongoing transition toward a more domestically supported carrier aviation ecosystem. The appearance of the J-35 would be another major highlight. The aircraft represents a significant step in the PLAN’s carrier aviation ambitions, bringing a fifth-generation stealth fighter capability into the carrier air wing. Its presence would provide another opportunity to examine the progress of China’s next-generation naval fighter program. Back in 2014, Zhuhai saw the public debut of the FC-31 fighter demonstrator. At the time, it was still a land-based concept, and export was the main talking point, although there was already speculation about a naval variant, today’s J-35. A People’s Liberation Army Navy J-35 fighter during trials from the carrier Fujian last year. Chinese internet via X Meanwhile, the KJ-600 is arguably one of the most important developments in the PLAN’s carrier aviation ecosystem. The twin-engine turboprop aircraft is designed to provide airborne early warning and battle management capabilities, something that would transform the situational awareness and coordination available to China’s carrier strike groups. One of the first high-definition photos of the KJ-600 carrier-based airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft. Chinese internet via X Several variants of the Z-20 family are also expected to feature, reflecting the growing importance of helicopters in carrier operations, including airborne anti-submarine warfare, utility, and other maritime support missions. You can read more about the Z-20 family and other Chinese rotary-wing developments in this previous TWZ deep-dive on the topic . A Z-20F, the anti-submarine warfare variant of the naval Z-20 family. Three more naval Z-20s are seen in the hangar behind, including a Z-20J shipborne transport and assault variant. Chinese internet via X Perhaps the most intriguing aircraft on the list, however, is the JL-15. The JL-15 is derived from the Hongdu JL-10, also exported as the L-15 Falcon, a twin-engine advanced jet trainer and lead-in fighter trainer. The navalized development was initially reported to be designated JL-10J, but is now confirmed as being the JL-15. A tailhook-equipped mockup was spotted alongside the aircraft carrier Fujian in 2024. However, its operational status remains unclear, and China is known to have encountered difficulties with its earlier JL-9G naval trainer, whose tailhook was reportedly deleted following structural problems. Regarding the rumoured JL-10J carrier-capable jet trainer, another hint was spotted next to the carrier Fujian: It appears to be an unfinished JL-10J mockup stored on the dockside . So question is: Two tails as shown in the latest CG or just one like the regular JL-10? pic.twitter.com/BM8W8MRGWK — @Rupprecht_A (@RupprechtDeino) March 19, 2024 Its appearance would provide a particularly interesting indication of how China is thinking about training its next generation of carrier-based pilots. A carrier-capable development of the JL-10 would be an important addition to the emerging carrier aviation ecosystem, bridging the gap between conventional jet training and the demanding requirements of operating from an aircraft carrier. The JL-15 also makes an interesting comparison with the U.S. Navy’s somewhat stuttering efforts to introduce a new training jet for its carrier pilots. The U.S. Navy’s Undergraduate Jet Training System (UJTS) program is intended to replace its aging fleet of T-45 Goshawk trainers, but the acquisition effort has encountered considerable difficulties. Earlier this month, we described how Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC) withdrew its proposed clean-sheet Freedom Jet from the competition, citing concerns over the Navy’s insistence on firm-fixed-price production commitments before the aircraft’s design had sufficiently matured. This leaves the Beechcraft M-346N , based on Leonardo’s established M-346 Master , as the only publicly known remaining contender . The program has also experienced schedule slippage, with the initial contract award now expected in the fourth quarter of Fiscal Year 2027. Perhaps more significant is the difference in the two services’ approaches to carrier aviation training. The U.S. Navy has removed the requirement for its next-generation jet trainer to be capable of operating from an actual aircraft carrier, including carrier qualification and simulated carrier touch-and-goes at land-based facilities. Instead, it increasingly relies on advanced simulation, virtualized training, and assisted carrier landing technologies to prepare pilots for the demands of carrier operations. The JL-15, by contrast, is intended to support carrier-based pilot training. A dedicated carrier-capable trainer could offer China a more direct pathway for preparing pilots for operations aboard its increasingly sophisticated — and expanding — carrier fleet. Taken together, the PLAN aircraft being lined up for Zhuhai this year illustrate the increasingly sophisticated and integrated nature of China’s carrier aviation ambitions . As well as the aircraft carriers and their embarked aircraft, these ambitions also require other surface and subsurface vessels to operate effectively. Uncrewed systems will form another important part of the display. The exhibition will include aerial drones, uncrewed underwater vehicles, and other autonomous platforms, reflecting the PLAN’s growing interest in the potential of uncrewed warfare. Chinese media reports suggest that the WZ-2 uncrewed helicopter will receive its public debut at Zhuhai, while the PLAN may well also want to capitalize on its recent announcement that it had successfully launched and recovered a GJ-21 stealthy flying-wing uncrewed combat air vehicle (UCAV) aboard the Type 076 amphibious assault ship Sichuan . GJ-21. Chinese internet via X A chance to see the GJ-21 up close would be a huge deal, but there are many other naval drone options that could be revealed in more detail. There are likely to be more navalized collaborative combat aircraft (CCA) concepts and developments, especially since the adoption of the electromagnetic aircraft launch system (EMALS) catapult opens up a huge range of possibilities for uncrewed aircraft operating as part of a carrier air wing. Potentially, these could include the mysterious MQ-25-like drone that we recently discussed , the role of which remains unclear. On top of that, constant CCA testing at locations such as Malan suggests there could be much more to discuss than just the systems officially highlighted. Many other naval drones will surely be on display as well, including lower-end attritable concepts. Beyond static displays, China’s navy plans to organize flight demonstrations, formation flights, and simulated operational exercises. Its stated aim is to highlight not only the capabilities of individual platforms but also their ability to operate together in complex maritime environments. Photos have emerged showing apparent rehearsals for the display, presenting examples of the J-15, J-35, and KJ-600 to represent Beijing’s broader carrier air wing ecosystem. Two J-15s, two J-35s, and a KJ-600 purportedly taking part in a rehearsal for a formation fly-over at Zhuhai. Chinese internet via X It is not immediately clear which versions of the J-15 are participating in this formation flight: they could be J-15Ts, but another possibility is the electronic warfare version, the J-15DT , that we have profiled in the past. Regardless, they highlight how China’s carrier aviation ambitions are increasingly focused on catapult-assisted takeoff but arrested recovery (CATOBAR) operations, which offer many advantages . The J-15DT electronic warfare version of the Chinese carrier Flanker is outfitted for operations aboard catapult-equipped flattops like the Fujian . Chinese internet via X For the first time, the exhibition will also include a substantial surface fleet component, making use of the docks at the nearby Gaolan Port. Among the vessels expected to be featured are the Type 075 amphibious assault ship, the Type 055 guided-missile destroyer, and the Type 054A guided-missile frigate. Their presence will offer a public-facing showcase of China’s increasingly sophisticated surface fleet and its expanding range of maritime capabilities. It should also be recalled that it was at Gaolan Port where at least one Chinese uncrewed surface vessel , a distinctive trimaran craft, was first spotted. The Type 055 guided-missile destroyer Nanchang sails during the naval exercise Joint Sea-2021 on October 19, 2021, in the Western part of the Pacific Ocean. Photo by Sun Zifa/China News Service via Getty Images The broader messaging surrounding the exhibition is also notable. According to the PLAN, this year’s displays will place greater emphasis on operational readiness and training, with active-duty equipment that regularly participates in exercises and maritime security missions taking precedence over purely exhibition-oriented displays. This should underscore how Beijing has rapidly spun up its naval capabilities, introducing new and more capable equipment that is increasingly capable of more sustained out-of-area operations. The expanded naval presence at Zhuhai looks set to provide a substantial public showcase of China’s ongoing naval modernization. As well as the combination of the J-15T, J-35, KJ-600, and Z-20 variants, the JL-15 points to an increasingly comprehensive carrier aviation enterprise. And, judging by previous editions of the show, there will almost certainly be more novelties on display as well.
